choices: The WHERE clause filters rows before grouping, and HAVING filters groups after aggregation — the query needs GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 10 with no WHERE on the count
WHERE can reference aggregate functions in Oracle if placed after GROUP BY
COUNT(*) in the WHERE clause is fine; the bug is the missing semicolon
Use ORDER BY instead of HAVING
evidence:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS c
FROM employees
WHERE COUNT(*) > 10
GROUP BY dept_id;
ORA-00934: group function is not allowed here
scenarios.hint: When does a group even exist for a filter to act on?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: A report should list departments with more than 10 employees. The query fails with ORA-00934.
scenarios.title: The aggregate in WHERE
scenarios.why: SQL evaluates in logical order: FROM → WHERE (row filter) → GROUP BY → HAVING (group filter) → SELECT → ORDER BY. Aggregates don't exist yet at WHERE time, hence ORA-00934. The fix: GROUP BY dept_id then HAVING COUNT(*) > 10. Remember: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups.

choices: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(commission_pct) counts non-NULL values only — the difference (e.g., 107 vs 35) tells you 72 employees have NULL commission
COUNT(*) is slower; always use COUNT(column) for performance
The two counts are identical; the discrepancy is a bug in the data
COUNT(commission_pct) includes NULLs, COUNT(*) excludes them
scenarios.hint: What does an aggregate function do when it meets a NULL?
scenarios.prompt: What does the difference prove about the data?
scenarios.situation: HR wants to know how many of 107 employees earn commission. A developer reports COUNT(*) = 107 and COUNT(commission_pct) = 35 and asks which is 'wrong'.
scenarios.title: The two counts
scenarios.why: All aggregate functions except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs. COUNT(*) = 107 rows; COUNT(commission_pct) = 35 non-NULL commissions, so 72 employees have NULL commission_pct. Neither is wrong — they answer different questions. This NULL-ignoring behavior is why AVG ignores NULLs too, and why NVL is needed before aggregating nullable columns.

choices: DISTINCT applies after SELECT projection but the duplicates differ in the unselected salary column — the rows are distinct once all selected columns are considered; to dedupe names only, use GROUP BY name or a subquery
DISTINCT is broken for VARCHAR2 columns in Oracle
Add ROWNUM = 1 to remove duplicates
DISTINCT only works on numeric columns
evidence: SELECT DISTINCT last_name, first_name FROM employees ORDER BY last_name;
... 'Smith' appears 3 times with different first names ...
scenarios.hint: DISTINCT dedupes what — the visible columns, or entire rows?
scenarios.situation: A query with SELECT DISTINCT still shows 'Smith' multiple times. The developer suspects DISTINCT is broken.
scenarios.title: The DISTINCT that didn't
scenarios.why: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows across the full select list — 'Smith, John' vs 'Smith, Jane' are different rows, so both survive. To get one row per last name, aggregate (GROUP BY last_name) or use a subquery/window function to pick a representative row. DISTINCT is row-level, never column-level.

choices: WHERE rownum <= 10 applies before ORDER BY — wrap in a subquery: SELECT * FROM (SELECT ... ORDER BY salary DESC) WHERE rownum <= 10; or use FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY
ROWNUM is 1-based, so use rownum < 10 for 10 rows
ORDER BY is ignored with ROWNUM; sorting is impossible in Oracle
Use rownum >= 1 AND rownum <= 10 after the ORDER BY
evidence: SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE rownum <= 3 ORDER BY salary DESC;
Three arbitrary mid-range salaries, not the top 3
scenarios.hint: ROWNUM is assigned when a row is fetched — before or after the sort?
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and why does the original fail?
scenarios.situation: A 'top 3 earners' report returns three random salaries instead of the highest. The query filters ROWNUM <= 3 with ORDER BY salary DESC.
scenarios.title: The top-N trap
scenarios.why: ROWNUM is a pseudocolumn assigned as rows are produced, before ORDER BY sorts them. So the filter grabs 3 arbitrary rows, then sorts those 3. The classic fix is a subquery (sort inside, filter ROWNUM outside); modern Oracle supports FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY. This is also why ROWNUM > n never matches — the first row must be 1.

choices: NULL values sort as largest by default in Oracle ascending order — NULL salaries appear last; use NULLS FIRST or NVL to control placement
NULLs are excluded from ORDER BY results
Oracle sorts NULLs first in ascending order by default
The ORDER BY is fine; NULLs indicate missing rows, not missing values
evidence: SELECT last_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;
Highest salaries first ... then rows with NULL salary at the end
scenarios.hint: Where does Oracle put NULLs in an ascending sort, and what does DESC do to that?
scenarios.prompt: Where will NULL salaries land, and how do you control it?
scenarios.situation: A salary ranking shows NULL-salary rows at the bottom of a DESC sort. The analyst wants them at the top flagged as 'unknown'.
scenarios.title: The NULL sort order
scenarios.why: Oracle treats NULL as the largest value for sorting: ASC puts NULLs last, DESC puts NULLs first — by default. NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST overrides this explicitly. NVL(salary, -1) is a hack; the explicit NULLS clause documents intent.

choices: SELECT list aliases are visible to ORDER BY but not to WHERE or GROUP BY — the query must repeat the expression or use a subquery/inline view
Aliases are visible to all clauses; the error is a typo
Oracle doesn't support aliases at all
Move the alias into the FROM clause
evidence: SELECT salary*12 AS annual FROM employees WHERE annual > 100000;
scenarios.hint: Which clauses run before the SELECT list is even computed?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the alias fail in WHERE but work in ORDER BY?
scenarios.situation: WHERE annual > 100000 raises ORA-00904, but ORDER BY annual works in the same query.
scenarios.title: The invisible alias
scenarios.why: Logical evaluation order strikes again: WHERE and GROUP BY execute before the SELECT list, so aliases don't exist yet; ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so aliases are visible. Fix by repeating the expression in WHERE, or wrapping in a subquery/inline view where the alias becomes a real column.

choices: A NULL department_id never satisfies the equality join — those employees vanish; use a LEFT JOIN from employees or handle NULLs explicitly
NULL department_id joins to every department with NULL id
The join will error on NULL keys
INNER JOIN treats NULL as equal to NULL
evidence: 5 employees have NULL department_id and are missing from the report
scenarios.hint: What does NULL = NULL evaluate to in SQL?
scenarios.prompt: Why are 5 employees missing, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: An employee/department report drops 5 employees. All 5 have NULL department_id.
scenarios.title: The vanishing employees
scenarios.why: NULL never equals anything, including NULL — so equality join conditions exclude NULL keys on both sides. LEFT JOIN keeps all employees (NULL department shows as NULL). This is the same reason NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns no rows: the anti-join predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN.

choices: EXISTS stops at the first match per row and is NULL-safe; IN builds the full list and breaks when the subquery returns NULL — prefer NOT EXISTS for anti-joins
IN is always faster than EXISTS in Oracle
NOT IN is NULL-safe; EXISTS is not
They are identical; the difference is stylistic
evidence:
SELECT last_name FROM employees
WHERE department_id NOT IN (SELECT department_id FROM departments);
0 rows — but departments has a row with NULL department_id
scenarios.hint: What happens to NOT IN when the list contains a NULL?
scenarios.prompt: Why does NOT IN return zero rows, and what is the robust alternative?
scenarios.situation: A 'employees in no department' report returns zero rows even though orphaned employees exist. The departments table contains one row with NULL department_id.
scenarios.title: The NOT IN that matched nothing
scenarios.why: NOT IN (list with NULL) → for each row, department_id NOT IN (…, NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN (because x <> NULL is UNKNOWN), and WHERE keeps only TRUE. Result: zero rows. NOT EXISTS uses a correlated predicate that stays NULL-safe, and EXISTS short-circuits on first match — also why EXISTS often outperforms IN on large sets.

choices: A correlated subquery referencing the outer query — for each employee, compare salary to the average of their own department
A non-correlated aggregate — AVG over the whole table gives the company average, not per-department
A self join on employee_id — compares each employee to themselves
GROUP BY in the outer query — it can't filter individual rows
scenarios.hint: The subquery must know 'which department am I comparing against' — where does that value come from?
scenarios.prompt: What kind of subquery does this require, and how does it work?
scenarios.situation: HR wants employees earning above their own department's average salary — a per-department comparison, not company-wide.
scenarios.title: The above-average club
scenarios.why: A correlated subquery references the outer query's row (e.department_id), so it re-evaluates per row with that row's department — giving a per-department average. A non-correlated subquery runs once (company-wide average). Correlated = per-row context; the trade-off is repeated execution, which is why EXISTS (short-circuit) often beats IN here.

choices: Self join: join employees to itself (manager/employee) ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id — one table, two roles via aliases
A subquery — self joins are not allowed in Oracle
UNION of the table with itself
A cross join filtered by ROWNUM
scenarios.hint: How do you put 'the same table' on both sides of a join?
scenarios.prompt: What join pattern models a hierarchy stored in one table?
scenarios.situation: The employees table has manager_id pointing to another employee's employee_id. The report needs each employee with their manager's name.
scenarios.title: The manager lookup
scenarios.why: A self join gives the table two aliases (e for employee, m for manager) and joins e.manager_id = m.employee_id. Aliases are mandatory — without them the query is ambiguous. This pattern also handles org-chart traversals (with CONNECT BY or recursive CTEs for multi-level).

choices: Scalar subquery in the SELECT list — one value per row; it must return exactly one row and one column or the query errors
A multi-row subquery in SELECT — Oracle concatenates the rows automatically
JOINs can't produce per-row aggregates
Scalar subqueries must be in the WHERE clause
evidence:
SELECT d.department_name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e
        WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id) AS headcount
FROM departments d;
scenarios.hint: How many rows may a subquery in the SELECT list return?
scenarios.prompt: What is this pattern called, and what is its hard constraint?
scenarios.situation: A department list needs a headcount column. A developer puts a COUNT(*) subquery in the SELECT list, correlated to each department.
scenarios.title: The count in the SELECT
scenarios.why: A scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column per outer row — correlated here to compute per-department headcount. If it returns 2+ rows: ORA-01427 'single-row subquery returns more than one row'. It runs per row (fine for small sets; a LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY scales better for large ones).

choices: The join condition is missing or wrong — it's a Cartesian product (every employee × every department); add ON e.department_id = d.department_id
The tables are too large; Oracle can't join them
Use UNION instead of JOIN for large tables
Add DISTINCT to fix the multiplication
evidence: SELECT e.last_name, d.department_name FROM employees e, departments d;
scenarios.hint: 107 × 27 = 2889. What join produces exactly rows(A) × rows(B)?
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: A 2-table report returns 2,889 rows from 107 employees and 27 departments. The old-style comma join has no WHERE clause.
scenarios.title: The exploding report
scenarios.why: Comma syntax without a join condition (or JOIN ... ON with no ON) is a cross join: every row × every row. 107 × 27 = 2,889 exactly. The fix is the join predicate e.department_id = d.department_id. DISTINCT would only mask it (and wrongly). In ANSI syntax, forgetting ON is a syntax error — one reason to prefer explicit JOIN syntax.

choices: The foreign key rejects the child row — insert the parent row first, or defer the constraint; the FK guarantees the parent exists at commit
Foreign keys only validate on SELECT, so the error is elsewhere
Disable the FK permanently — it's just documentation
Insert the child first; Oracle auto-creates the parent
evidence:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_cust
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id);
ORA-02291: integrity constraint (FK_CUST) violated - parent key not found
scenarios.hint: What does a foreign key promise about the parent row?
scenarios.prompt: What does ORA-02291 mean, and what are the legitimate fixes?
scenarios.situation: An order insert fails with ORA-02291. The customer_id doesn't exist in customers yet.
scenarios.title: The orphan order
scenarios.why: A foreign key enforces that every child value exists in the parent key — the child can't precede the parent. Legit fixes: insert parent first (normal flow), or define the constraint DEFERRABLE and SET CONSTRAINTS DEFERRED to validate at commit. Disabling the FK destroys the guarantee; Oracle never auto-creates parents.

choices: TRUNCATE is DDL — it deallocates storage, resets high-water mark, can't be rolled back granularly, and fires no DELETE triggers; use DELETE for selective/audited removal
TRUNCATE and DELETE are identical except speed
TRUNCATE can have a WHERE clause in Oracle 19c+
DELETE can't be used on large tables
scenarios.hint: Which one is DDL and which is DML — and what does that imply for triggers and rollback?
scenarios.prompt: What are the behavioral differences that matter?
scenarios.situation: A nightly job 'clears' a staging table with TRUNCATE. Audit triggers on the table never fire, and a DBA warns the operation can't be undone the way DELETE can.
scenarios.title: The midnight truncate
scenarios.why: TRUNCATE TABLE is DDL: it drops storage segments (fast, resets the high-water mark), issues an implicit commit, fires no row triggers, and can't be rolled back statement-by-statement. DELETE is DML: row-by-row, trigger-firing, WHERE-capable, and rollback-able. Choose TRUNCATE for full-table resets, DELETE when you need selectivity, triggers, or transactional control.

choices: Update the existing rows to valid values (or NULL if allowed) first, then add the constraint; or add it NOVALIDATE and validate later after cleanup
Constraints can only be added to empty tables
Drop the table and recreate it with the constraint
Add the constraint DISABLED permanently
evidence: ALTER TABLE employees ADD CONSTRAINT chk_sal CHECK (salary > 0);
ORA-02293: cannot validate (CHK_SAL) - check constraint violated
scenarios.hint: The constraint validates existing rows too — how do you deal with legacy data?
scenarios.prompt: How do you add a constraint to a table with legacy violations?
scenarios.situation: Adding CHECK (salary > 0) fails with ORA-02293 because old rows contain 0/negative salaries.
scenarios.title: The legacy data problem
scenarios.why: ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT validates all existing rows by default. Options: clean the data first (UPDATE to valid values), or add the constraint NOVALIDATE (enforced for new DML only) and later validate after cleanup. NOVALIDATE is the pragmatic path for huge tables; ENABLE VALIDATE is the strict end state.

choices: MERGE — single statement with WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE / WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT; atomic and avoids the race between the check and the write
SELECT then INSERT in two statements — the gap is harmless
INSERT with a WHERE NOT EXISTS in a loop — same thing
MERGE can only update, not insert
evidence: Nightly sync: update existing product rows, insert new ones, in one atomic operation
scenarios.hint: Which single statement does 'update if exists, insert if not' atomically?
scenarios.prompt: Which statement implements the sync, and why is it better than check-then-act?
scenarios.situation: A nightly feed must update existing products and insert new ones. The current SELECT-then-INSERT/UPDATE has race conditions under concurrency.
scenarios.title: The nightly upsert
scenarios.why: MERGE joins source to target and applies WHEN MATCHED (UPDATE) and WHEN NOT MATCHED (INSERT) in one statement — one pass, atomic, no check-then-act race. The two-statement pattern can double-insert under concurrency. MERGE also supports DELETE clauses and is the standard upsert in Oracle.

choices: DEFAULT ON NULL (or a BEFORE INSERT trigger / identity column) — a plain DEFAULT only applies when the column is omitted, not when NULL is explicitly inserted
DEFAULT applies to explicit NULLs too; the app is wrong
NOT NULL prevents explicit NULLs automatically
Use a CHECK constraint to convert NULLs
evidence:
CREATE TABLE t (id NUMBER DEFAULT 100, name VARCHAR2(20));
INSERT INTO t (id, name) VALUES (NULL, 'x');
scenarios.hint: When does DEFAULT fire — on omitted columns, or on explicit NULLs?
scenarios.prompt: Why is id NULL, and what are the fixes?
scenarios.situation: A column has DEFAULT 100, but explicit NULL inserts stay NULL. The developer expected the default.
scenarios.title: The default that didn't
scenarios.why: DEFAULT fires only when the column is omitted from the INSERT list. An explicit NULL is a real value — it stays NULL. Fixes: DEFAULT ON NULL (12c+, treats explicit NULL as 'use default'), a NOT NULL constraint to reject it, an identity column (GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY) for surrogate keys, or a trigger. Know the distinction: omitted vs. explicit NULL.

choices: A sequence (or identity column) with NOCACHE risk of gaps — gaps are normal (rollbacks, cache loss, RAC); never use sequences for gapless numbering
Sequences guarantee gapless numbers; the gaps are a bug
Use MAX(id)+1 in the application — it's gapless and safe
Gaps mean the sequence is corrupted; rebuild it
evidence: CREATE SEQUENCE order_seq START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 1 CACHE 20;
scenarios.hint: What happens to cached sequence values when the instance crashes or a transaction rolls back?
scenarios.prompt: Are the gaps a problem, and what is the rule about sequences?
scenarios.situation: Order numbers from a sequence show gaps (1001, 1002, 1005...). Finance asks if numbers are being 'lost'.
scenarios.title: The missing order numbers
scenarios.why: Sequence gaps are expected and harmless: cached values are lost on instance failure, rolled-back transactions don't return values, and RAC nodes allocate ranges. Sequences guarantee uniqueness and ordering-ish, never gaplessness. For gapless numbering (invoices, legal docs), you need serialized custom logic — MAX(id)+1 is a concurrency disaster. The rule: sequences for keys, custom logic for gapless documents.

choices: COALESCE — returns the first non-NULL; NVL evaluates both arguments always (and requires matching types), so COALESCE is safer with expensive/side-effect expressions
NVL — it short-circuits like COALESCE
They are identical; NVL is just shorter
DECODE — it's the only NULL-safe option
evidence:
SELECT NVL(expensive_fn(x), 0) FROM t;  -- slow even when x is not null
SELECT COALESCE(x, expensive_fn(y), 0) FROM t;  -- fast
scenarios.hint: Which one evaluates its arguments lazily, left to right?
scenarios.prompt: Which function fits, and what is the evaluation difference?
scenarios.situation: A query uses NVL(x, expensive_function(y)) and is slow even when x is never NULL. The developer assumes NVL skips the second argument.
scenarios.title: The slow NVL
scenarios.why: NVL always evaluates both arguments — no short-circuit — and requires compatible types. COALESCE (ANSI standard) evaluates left-to-right and stops at the first non-NULL, and takes N arguments. For fallback chains or expensive defaults, COALESCE is the correct tool; NVL is fine for simple two-value defaults.

choices: MONTHS_BETWEEN gives fractional months — TRUNC it for complete months, and use ADD_MONTHS for date arithmetic; direct subtraction gives days
Subtracting dates gives months in Oracle
MONTHS_BETWEEN returns an integer always
Use SYSDATE - hire_date and divide by 12
scenarios.hint: Date minus date = ? And what unit does MONTHS_BETWEEN return?
scenarios.prompt: How do you compute 'complete months of service' correctly?
scenarios.situation: HR needs complete months between hire_date and today. MONTHS_BETWEEN returns 8.58, and the developer rounds it — sometimes over-crediting tenure.
scenarios.title: The fractional tenure
scenarios.why: Date1 - Date2 = days (fractional). MONTHS_BETWEEN = fractional months. For complete months: TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(...)). For date math: ADD_MONTHS(date, n) handles month-end correctly (Jan 31 + 1 month = Feb 28/29). Never do tenure math by dividing days by 30.

choices: SUBSTR with INSTR — INSTR finds the 2nd delimiter position, SUBSTR extracts between; or REGEXP_SUBSTR for pattern-based parsing
LIKE can extract substrings directly
SUBSTR alone with fixed positions — delimiters never move
SPLIT_PART — the Oracle string-splitting function
scenarios.hint: Which function locates the Nth occurrence of a delimiter?
scenarios.prompt: How do you extract the 2nd segment robustly?
scenarios.situation: Product codes like 'ELEC-TV-48-2026' need the 2nd segment extracted. Fixed-position SUBSTR breaks when the first segment varies in length.
scenarios.title: The shifting segments
scenarios.why: INSTR(string, '-', 1, 2) finds the 2nd delimiter; SUBSTR between the 1st and 2nd gives the segment regardless of length. REGEXP_SUBSTR(code, '[^-]+', 1, 2) does it in one call. (Oracle has no SPLIT_PART — that's Postgres.) Fixed positions are fragile; delimiter-relative parsing is robust.

choices: CASE — ANSI standard, readable, handles searched conditions; DECODE is Oracle-specific and only does equality
DECODE — it handles ranges and inequalities
CASE can't be used in ORDER BY
DECODE is ANSI standard
scenarios.hint: Which construct supports 'WHEN amount > 1000 THEN ...' — equality-only, or full conditions?
scenarios.prompt: Which should the team standardize on, and why?
scenarios.situation: A query uses DECODE for status labels. A new rule needs a range condition (amount > 1000), which DECODE can't express.
scenarios.title: The DECODE ceiling
scenarios.why: DECODE only does equality comparisons — it's Oracle-proprietary shorthand. CASE (simple and searched forms) is ANSI, supports any condition (ranges, NULL checks, compound predicates), and nests cleanly. Standardize on CASE; DECODE remains only for legacy compatibility.

choices: TO_CHAR(date, 'YYYY-MM-DD') for display; never rely on implicit conversion or NLS settings — explicit format models are deterministic
Implicit conversion is fine; NLS_DATE_FORMAT is always 'YYYY-MM-DD'
TO_DATE on an already-date value to 'normalize' it
Store dates as VARCHAR2 to control the format
evidence: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date = '03-10-2026'; -- works in dev, fails in prod
scenarios.hint: What does '03-10-2026' mean — March 10 or October 3? It depends on what?
scenarios.prompt: Why does it work in dev but fail in prod?
scenarios.situation: A date literal '03-10-2026' works in dev but raises errors in prod. The NLS_DATE_FORMAT differs between environments.
scenarios.title: The date that changed meaning
scenarios.why: Implicit string-to-date conversion uses the session's NLS_DATE_FORMAT — environment-dependent, so '03-10-2026' is ambiguous (DD-MM vs MM-DD). Explicit TO_DATE('2026-10-03','YYYY-MM-DD') or ANSI DATE '2026-10-03' literals are deterministic. Rule: explicit format models everywhere; never store dates as strings.

choices: ROUND for rounding, TRUNC for truncation toward zero — ROUND(8.58, 0) = 9, TRUNC(8.58, 0) = 8; and CEIL/FLOOR for directional rounding
ROUND and TRUNC are identical
TRUNC rounds to nearest; ROUND truncates
Use CAST to round numbers
evidence: SELECT ROUND(8.58,0), TRUNC(8.58,0), CEIL(8.2), FLOOR(8.9) FROM dual;
scenarios.hint: One rounds to nearest, one chops — which is which?
scenarios.prompt: What does each function do, and when does the difference matter?
scenarios.situation: A billing calc needs 'round half up' for invoices but 'drop fractions' for loyalty points. The developer uses them interchangeably.
scenarios.title: The rounding mixup
scenarios.why: ROUND(n, d) rounds to nearest (half away from zero by default); TRUNC(n, d) truncates toward zero — chops decimals. CEIL goes up, FLOOR goes down. Money: ROUND. 'Complete units' logic: TRUNC or FLOOR. Mixing them silently misprices things.

choices: Add an EXCEPTION block handling NO_DATA_FOUND (and TOO_MANY_ROWS) — SELECT INTO must return exactly one row; unhandled exceptions propagate to the caller and roll back to the last commit
SELECT INTO returns NULL when no rows match — no exception needed
Wrap it in a loop — loops suppress exceptions
Exceptions in PL/SQL are only warnings
scenarios.hint: SELECT INTO demands exactly one row — what are the two ways that demand can fail?
scenarios.prompt: What must the block handle, and what happens if it doesn't?
scenarios.situation: A lookup block fails with ORA-01403 when the ID doesn't exist. There's no EXCEPTION section.
scenarios.title: The unhandled lookup
scenarios.why: SELECT INTO requires exactly one row: zero rows → NO_DATA_FOUND (ORA-01403), multiple → TOO_MANY_ROWS. Without an EXCEPTION handler, the error propagates up, aborting the block and rolling back uncommitted work to the last COMMIT. Handle the expected cases explicitly; let truly unexpected errors propagate.

choices: %TYPE (and %ROWTYPE) anchor variables to table definitions — if the column widens, the code adapts without edits
%TYPE is documentation only; it doesn't affect the datatype
Hardcode VARCHAR2(50) — table definitions never change
Use NUMBER for all variables to be safe
scenarios.hint: What breaks first when the DBA widens last_name from 50 to 100?
scenarios.situation: A DBA widens employees.last_name to 100 chars. Blocks with hardcoded VARCHAR2(50) start truncating; blocks using %TYPE are unaffected.
scenarios.title: The widened column
scenarios.why: %TYPE binds a variable's datatype to a table column; %ROWTYPE binds a record to a whole row. Schema changes propagate automatically — no code edits, no truncation bugs. Hardcoded types create a hidden contract with the DDL that breaks silently. Anchor to the dictionary.

choices: BULK COLLECT with FORALL — fetch in batches and apply DML in bulk; row-by-row context switches between PL/SQL and SQL engines kill performance
Add a COMMIT inside the loop — commits speed up loops
Row-by-row is fine; the engines are the same
Use a cursor FOR loop with an inner SELECT per row
scenarios.hint: Every loop iteration crosses an engine boundary — how do you cross it once per thousand rows instead?
scenarios.prompt: What is the performance pattern, and why is the loop slow?
scenarios.situation: A 2M-row migration loop runs for hours. Each iteration does one SELECT-via-cursor and one UPDATE — millions of PL/SQL↔SQL context switches.
scenarios.title: The hours-long loop
scenarios.why: Row-by-row processing pays a context switch per iteration between the PL/SQL and SQL engines. BULK COLLECT fetches batches into collections; FORALL sends DML as array operations — one switch per batch. Typical speedup: orders of magnitude. (Committing inside the loop doesn't speed anything and breaks restartability.)

choices: The exception in the inner block propagates to the outer EXCEPTION handler after the inner block ends — inner handlers catch first, unhandled exceptions bubble outward
The inner exception is swallowed automatically
Propagation stops at the first BEGIN
Outer handlers can't see inner exceptions
evidence:
BEGIN  -- outer
  BEGIN  -- inner
    risky_call;  -- raises APP_ERROR
  END;  -- no handler here
EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN log_it; END;
scenarios.hint: If nobody catches it inside, where does it go?
scenarios.prompt: Where does the inner exception end up?
scenarios.situation: A nested block raises an error with no inner handler. The developer expects it to vanish; instead the outer handler logs it.
scenarios.title: The bubbling error
scenarios.why: Exceptions propagate outward through enclosing blocks until a matching handler is found; unhandled at the top, they reach the client. WHEN OTHERS should log and re-raise (RAISE) rather than swallow — swallowing hides bugs. Design: handle what you can meaningfully recover from, let the rest bubble.

choices: Implicit cursor FOR loop — Oracle opens, fetches, and closes automatically; explicit cursors are for when you need manual control (parameters, early exit, %NOTFOUND checks)
Explicit cursors are always faster
Implicit cursors can't be used with SELECT
FOR loops require explicit OPEN/CLOSE
scenarios.hint: Who opens and closes the cursor here — you, or the loop?
scenarios.prompt: Why is this the idiomatic pattern, and when would you go explicit?
scenarios.situation: A code review flags a cursor FOR loop as 'hiding the cursor'. The author claims it's the standard idiom.
scenarios.title: The hidden cursor
scenarios.why: The cursor FOR loop is the idiomatic implicit cursor: Oracle handles OPEN/FETCH/CLOSE, it's concise and leak-proof. Explicit cursors (DECLARE/CURSOR/OPEN/FETCH/CLOSE) are for manual control — parameterized cursors, fetching in batches with LIMIT, or checking %ROWCOUNT/%NOTFOUND mid-stream. Default to the FOR loop; go explicit when you need the steering wheel.

choices: Use autonomous transaction (PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION) for the log insert with its own COMMIT — the audit record persists even when the main transaction rolls back
COMMIT before the risky work — the log is safe then
Logging to a table is impossible during a rollback
Write logs to DBMS_OUTPUT — output survives rollback
evidence: Audit log of attempted operations must survive even when the business transaction rolls back
scenarios.hint: Which pragma gives a block its own transaction, independent of the caller?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make audit records rollback-proof?
scenarios.situation: An audit table logs who attempted what. When the main transaction rolls back, the audit rows vanish too — defeating the audit.
scenarios.title: The vanishing audit trail
scenarios.why: An autonomous transaction (PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION) runs in its own transaction context: it can COMMIT independently, so audit rows persist even if the caller rolls back. Use sparingly and only for logging — overuse breaks transactional integrity. DBMS_OUTPUT is session output, not a durable audit.

choices: Package spec declares the public interface; the body implements it — callers depend on the spec, so body changes don't invalidate dependents; also enables overloading and session state
Specs are optional; put everything in the body
Packages can't be changed without dropping callers
The body is public and the spec is private
scenarios.hint: Which part do callers compile against — the declaration or the implementation?
scenarios.prompt: What is the architectural benefit of the spec/body split?
scenarios.situation: A team debates whether the spec/body split is ceremony. They currently ship standalone procedures.
scenarios.title: The spec/body split
scenarios.why: The spec is the contract: public procedures, types, constants. Dependents compile against the spec, so body-only changes (bug fixes, optimization) don't invalidate them — huge for large systems. Packages also group related logic, support overloading, and hold session-persistent state.

choices: BEFORE EACH ROW trigger validating/transforming the incoming row (e.g., uppercasing, defaulting) — row-level fires per row; statement-level fires once per statement
AFTER STATEMENT trigger — it sees each row's values
A CHECK constraint can't validate formats; only triggers can
INSTEAD OF trigger on the base table
evidence: Every inserted email must be lowercased and validated for '@' before it lands; bulk inserts of 10k rows must all be checked
scenarios.hint: Per-row or per-statement — which granularity sees each new row's values?
scenarios.prompt: Which trigger timing and granularity, and why?
scenarios.situation: Email addresses must be normalized and validated on every insert, including bulk loads.
scenarios.title: The email normalizer
scenarios.why: BEFORE EACH ROW fires once per row before the insert — it can modify :NEW values (lowercase the email) and raise errors to reject bad rows. Statement-level triggers fire once per statement and can't see row values. AFTER ROW can't modify :NEW (it's already written). Granularity + timing must match the job.

choices: Mutating-table error — a row trigger can't query its own table; use a compound trigger (collect row IDs, process after statement) or a statement-level trigger
The trigger is too slow; add an index
Mutating errors are warnings; ignore them
Move the query into an autonomous transaction inside the trigger
evidence:
CREATE TRIGGER trg_emp AFTER INSERT ON employees FOR EACH ROW
DECLARE v_c NUMBER; BEGIN
  SELECT COUNT(*) INTO v_c FROM employees; -- ORA-04091
END;
scenarios.hint: The table is mid-change while the trigger runs — why can't it be read consistently?
scenarios.prompt: What is ORA-04091, and what is the correct pattern?
scenarios.situation: A row trigger queries its own table and fails with ORA-04091.
scenarios.title: The trigger that read its own table
scenarios.why: During row-level trigger execution the table is 'mutating' — mid-DML, in an inconsistent state — so Oracle forbids querying it (prevents seeing partial changes). The sanctioned pattern: compound trigger — collect :NEW keys in the row section, query/process in the AFTER STATEMENT section when the table is stable. (Autonomous-transaction workarounds see uncommitted data — a correctness hazard.)

choices: Move the logic to a procedure called explicitly, or use a view with INSTEAD OF trigger only where a view is genuinely needed — business logic in triggers hides behavior and complicates debugging
More triggers — split the logic across five triggers for clarity
Triggers are the only place business logic can live in Oracle
Disable constraints; triggers replace them
scenarios.hint: If the logic only runs when someone remembers the trigger exists, who owns it?
scenarios.prompt: What is the architectural guidance on triggers vs. procedures?
scenarios.situation: Critical pricing logic lives in three triggers. New developers don't know it exists; bugs surface as 'the database changed my data'.
scenarios.title: The hidden business logic
scenarios.why: Triggers fire implicitly — invisible at the call site — making behavior surprising and hard to debug, with ordering and recursion hazards. Guidance: keep triggers for auditing, simple validation/defaulting, and enforcing invariants close to data; put business workflows in named, explicitly-called procedures/packages. INSTEAD OF triggers belong on views (making non-updatable views updatable), not as logic-hiding on tables.

choices: Package state (variables/constants in the body) persists for the session — great for caching, dangerous when code assumes fresh state across calls
Package variables reset after every statement
State is shared across all sessions
Packages can't hold state
scenarios.hint: How long does a package variable live — a call, or the session?
scenarios.prompt: What is the lifecycle of package state, and what is the risk?
scenarios.situation: A package caches 'last processed ID' in a body variable. It works in testing, but in production with connection pooling, stale values leak between logical users.
scenarios.title: The sticky package variable
scenarios.why: Package variables persist for the database session — surviving across calls. In pooled environments, one physical session serves many logical users, so leftover state leaks. Use package state deliberately (caches with explicit invalidation), never as implicit cross-call memory. SERIALLY_REUSABLE pragma is the opt-out for stateless packages.

choices: Compile-time dependency chain — altering the procedure invalidates dependents; Oracle auto-recompiles on next use, but check USER_OBJECTS/DBA_OBJECTS for INVALID and recompile explicitly in deployments
Invalid objects fix themselves instantly with no risk
Dependencies don't exist in Oracle
Drop and recreate everything on each deploy
evidence:
ALTER PROCEDURE calc_bonus COMPILE; -- succeeds
-- but 4 views and 2 triggers are now INVALID
scenarios.hint: What happens to objects that reference a changed procedure?
scenarios.prompt: What happened to the dependents, and what is the deployment discipline?
scenarios.situation: After altering a procedure, dependent views and triggers show INVALID. The deploy script declares success.
scenarios.title: The invalid dependents
scenarios.why: Oracle tracks dependencies: changing a procedure's signature invalidates dependents. They auto-recompile on next access, but a runtime recompile failure becomes a production error — so deployments should explicitly recompile and verify (UTL_RECOMP, DBMS_UTILITY.COMPILE_SCHEMA) and check for INVALID objects. Signature changes are breaking changes; body-only changes via package bodies avoid invalidation.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Oracle Sql as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The SELECT Deep Dive Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that SELECT Deep Dive is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in SELECT Deep Dive?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — SELECT Deep Dive issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — SELECT Deep Dive is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is SELECT Deep Dive supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any SELECT Deep Dive failure in Oracle Sql.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to SELECT Deep Dive
evidence: All SELECT Deep Dive components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Start Here
domains.description: How to use this bootcamp, study strategy for the Oracle SQL certification exam, and the SQL lab environment guide.

scenarios.title: Navigating the bootcamp
scenarios.situation: You're new to Oracle SQL and want certification in 8 weeks, studying 6 hours a week.
scenarios.prompt: What's the right first two weeks?
choices: Start-here (all 4 lessons), then SELECT and joins/subqueries in order — SELECT semantics underlie every later domain; build the trap list from day one
Jump to performance tuning — it's the most advanced
Take mock assessments first to benchmark
Read all lessons across 15 domains before running SQL
scenarios.why: Dependency order dominates SQL learning: SELECT and joins are prerequisites for everything after, and they're the exam's heaviest weight. Front-loading them is both pedagogically and strategically correct.
scenarios.hint: Which domains do all the others assume?
evidence: start-here -> SELECT -> joins -> DDL/DML -> functions -> PL/SQL

scenarios.title: Planning study time
scenarios.situation: You have 6 hours a week. You want to pass, not just learn.
choices: Cram everything in the last two weeks
2h lessons, 2h labs, 2h scenarios — the exam tests query judgment under options, and scenarios train exactly that; labs build the execution intuition that makes query questions fast
6h of lessons; labs later
All scenarios, no lessons
scenarios.why: The exam is query-heavy: 'which query returns X' rewards practiced judgment. An even three-way split builds knowledge (lessons), intuition (labs), and judgment (scenarios) together.
scenarios.hint: What question shape dominates the exam?
evidence: Lessons + labs + scenarios in balance; judgment is trained

scenarios.title: Using labs effectively
scenarios.situation: A lab asks you to write a top-N-per-group query, but you've only read about analytic functions.
choices: Skip the lab — scenarios matter more
Copy the example verbatim
Do the lab now — run the example, break it (wrong function, missing partition), fix it; the fix cycle is where analytic thinking forms
Re-read the lessons until confident
scenarios.why: Labs convert syntax knowledge into query intuition, and deliberate breaking builds debugging skill. The exam's query questions reward those who've seen queries fail and fixed them.
scenarios.hint: When does query intuition actually form?
evidence: Run, break, fix — every example, every lab

scenarios.title: Mock exam strategy
scenarios.situation: First mock: 68%. The exam needs ~65-70%. Three weeks left.
choices: Take a mock every day until it clicks
Memorize the mock questions
Focus on your strongest families
Analyze misses by family — drill the two weakest families fully (lessons + labs + scenarios), add each miss's rule to the trap list, then re-mock; targeted loops beat blanket review
scenarios.why: Miss analysis by family turns a score into a study plan. Each miss becomes a trap-list rule, so the list compounds. Daily mocks without review just rehearse the same gaps.
scenarios.hint: What does a miss become in your system?
evidence: Miss -> family drill -> trap-list rule -> re-mock

domains.name: Mock Assessment
domains.description: Timed assessment shell — scenarios are drawn from all domains at runtime.

domains.name: Capstone: Analytics Mart
domains.description: Design and build a complete analytics data mart: schema, ETL, queries, and performance tuning on Oracle.

scenarios.title: Capstone: grain decision
scenarios.situation: Phase 1: stakeholders say 'we need order analytics'. You must define the fact grain.
choices: Declare the grain explicitly ('one row per order line item') and get sign-off — every dimension, measure, and query hangs off the grain; an undeclared grain produces an unqueryable mart
One row per order (headers only)
One row per customer per day
Load the source tables as-is
scenarios.why: The grain statement is the mart's constitution: it determines what's analyzable. Line-item grain supports both order and line questions; header grain can't answer line questions. Decide deliberately, document, sign off.
scenarios.hint: What breaks if the grain is wrong?
evidence: Grain declared and signed off before any DDL

scenarios.title: Capstone: changing dimensions
scenarios.situation: Customer regions change occasionally; history by current region is acceptable.
choices: Ignore changes
Type 1 (overwrite) — history by current region is acceptable, so overwrite is correct and simplest; document the choice and its implication (historical reports reflect current regions)
Type 2 (version rows) — always
Type 3 (previous value column)
scenarios.why: SCD choice follows the history requirement: 'current region acceptable' means Type 1. Type 2 adds versioning complexity for history nobody asked for. The rationale, documented, is the deliverable.
scenarios.hint: What requirement would force Type 2?
evidence: History requirement decides the type; document the trade

scenarios.title: Capstone: load failure
scenarios.situation: Nightly load failed at the fact step; dimensions loaded fine. It's 7 AM; reports run at 8.
choices: Manually insert the missing rows
Check the control table + error log, fix the fact-step issue, rerun from the fact step only (idempotent design) — staging and step-wise loads make partial reruns safe; don't reload dimensions
Reload everything from scratch
Skip today's reports
scenarios.why: Step-wise idempotent loads enable surgical recovery: dimensions are already correct, so rerunning them wastes time and risks duplication. The control table tells you exactly where to resume.
scenarios.hint: What design enables the partial rerun?
evidence: Staged, logged, idempotent steps -> surgical recovery

scenarios.title: Capstone: slow dashboard
scenarios.situation: The monthly-sales dashboard takes 40 seconds; it aggregates 50M fact rows.
choices: Cache the dashboard for a day
Aggregate in the application
Materialized view pre-aggregating monthly sales, refreshed on load — the dashboard queries thousands of rows instead of 50M; verify the refresh schedule matches data freshness needs
Bigger database server
scenarios.why: Pre-aggregation is the structural fix for repeated heavy aggregation — the MV refreshes once per load, dashboards read the summary. Bigger servers don't fix algorithmic waste; caching masks staleness questions.
scenarios.hint: What determines the MV refresh schedule?
evidence: Pre-aggregate repeated heavy queries; schedule to freshness needs

scenarios.title: Capstone: the demo
scenarios.situation: Demo day: 5 minutes to show the mart to stakeholders.
choices: All 10 queries rapid-fire
One business question -> the query -> the answer, twice (a KPI and a trend), then the architecture slide — stakeholders remember answers, not schemas; the demo proves the mart does its job
Full ER diagram walkthrough
Live ETL run
scenarios.why: Demos sell outcomes: question-to-answer twice proves value, the architecture slide proves solidity. Schema tours and ETL runs are engineer-to-engineer content for a different meeting.
scenarios.hint: What do stakeholders remember from demos?
evidence: Question -> query -> answer, twice; architecture last

domains.name: Advanced Queries
domains.description: Window functions, CTEs, PIVOT, hierarchical queries, and complex analytical SQL.

scenarios.title: Top-N per group
scenarios.situation: Report: top 2 earners per department, ties included — if two people tie for 2nd, both appear.
choices: FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY with PARTITION BY
ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 2 per department

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) in a subquery, filter rn <= 2 in the outer query — wait, ROW_NUMBER breaks ties arbitrarily; use RANK() to keep ties: RANK() OVER (...) then rk <= 2
SELECT ... WHERE ROWNUM <= 2 GROUP BY department_id
scenarios.why: Top-N per group = analytic rank in a subquery + filter outside (analytics can't go in WHERE). Ties-included means RANK/DENSE_RANK, not ROW_NUMBER — ROW_NUMBER would arbitrarily drop a tied 2nd place. The corrected choice names the right function.
scenarios.hint: Which ranking function keeps ties, and where can analytics appear?
evidence: RANK() in subquery, filter outside; ROW_NUMBER drops ties

scenarios.title: Finding gaps in a sequence
scenarios.situation: Invoice numbers should be consecutive. Find the missing ones in a 2M-row table.
choices: COUNT(*) vs MAX(id) - MIN(id) + 1 only tells you a gap exists, not where
LAG(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) to compare each row to its predecessor; where id - prev_id > 1, the gap is (prev_id+1 .. id-1) — single pass, no self-join
Self-join the table to itself on id = id + 1
Export to a spreadsheet and eyeball it
scenarios.why: LAG gives the predecessor per row in one ordered pass; the arithmetic exposes each gap's bounds. Self-joins on 2M rows are brutal; the count trick detects but doesn't locate.
scenarios.hint: What single-pass analytic exposes each gap's location?
evidence: LAG(id) OVER (ORDER BY id); gap where id - prev > 1

scenarios.title: Safe dedup
scenarios.situation: The customers table has duplicates on email. Keep the most recently updated row per email, delete the rest — 500K rows, production table.
choices: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY updated_at DESC) as rn, then DELETE WHERE rn > 1 — deterministic survivor per email, one statement
DELETE with a NOT IN subquery on email
CREATE TABLE AS SELECT DISTINCT, drop the original
Delete all duplicates then re-insert one copy from backup
scenarios.why: The ROW_NUMBER partition defines 'duplicate set' and the ORDER BY picks the survivor deterministically; the delete is one statement, auditable via SELECT first. CTAS-drop loses constraints/indexes/grants; NOT IN risks the NULL trap.
scenarios.hint: How do you pick exactly one survivor per duplicate set?
evidence: ROW_NUMBER partition by key, order by keep-priority, delete rn>1

scenarios.title: Org chart levels
scenarios.situation: HR wants the org chart: name indented by depth, each person's top-level executive, sorted properly within each level.
choices: A self-join repeated 5 times for 5 levels
CONNECT BY without START WITH
ORDER BY name on a hierarchical query
START WITH manager_id IS NULL CONNECT BY PRIOR employee_id = manager_id, SELECT LEVEL, LPAD + CONNECT_BY_ROOT, ORDER SIBLINGS BY name — hierarchy, depth, root, and level-preserving sort in one
scenarios.why: START WITH roots the tree; PRIOR walks parent->child; LEVEL gives depth; CONNECT_BY_ROOT carries the executive down; ORDER SIBLINGS BY sorts within levels without flattening. Fixed-depth self-joins break at level 6.
scenarios.hint: Which clause sorts within levels without flattening the tree?
evidence: START WITH root, CONNECT BY PRIOR, ORDER SIBLINGS BY

scenarios.title: Quarterly crosstab
scenarios.situation: Sales rows: (product, quarter, amount). Finance wants one row per product with Q1..Q4 columns.
choices: Export and pivot in a spreadsheet
GROUP BY product, quarter and let the app pivot
PIVOT (SUM(amount) FOR quarter IN ('Q1','Q2','Q3','Q4')) — declarative rotation, IN list defines the columns
Four separate queries UNIONed
scenarios.why: PIVOT is the declarative answer: the FOR...IN list becomes columns, the aggregate fills cells. UNION-of-four is four scans; app-side pivoting moves database work to the network.
scenarios.hint: What defines the output columns of a PIVOT?
evidence: PIVOT (agg FOR col IN (...)) — IN list = columns

scenarios.title: Year-over-year growth
scenarios.situation: Monthly revenue per region. Compute YoY growth % per region per month in one query.
choices: LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month) as prior_year, then (revenue - prior_year)/prior_year — 12-month lookback aligned by region
Self-join on month = month - 12
Twelve separate queries, one per lag
AVG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region)
scenarios.why: LAG with offset 12 partitioned by region peers each month with the same month last year in one pass; the division gives growth %. The self-join works but scans twice; the plain average isn't YoY at all.
scenarios.hint: How do you align 'same month last year' in one pass?
evidence: LAG(x, 12) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month)

scenarios.title: Data quality audit
scenarios.situation: Audit: find all employee emails that are NOT valid format, and extract the domain of the valid ones for a provider report.
choices: CHECK constraint only — the bad data is already there
WHERE NOT REGEXP_LIKE(email, '^[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$') for invalid; REGEXP_SUBSTR(email, '@(.+)$', 1, 1, NULL, 1) for domains — validation plus extraction
LIKE '%@%' for validation; SUBSTR for domains
Export and check in a script
scenarios.why: REGEXP_LIKE with anchored pattern is the real validation (LIKE '%@%' passes 'a@b'); REGEXP_SUBSTR with a capture group extracts the domain. CHECK constraints prevent future bad data but don't find existing violations.
scenarios.hint: Why is LIKE '%@%' insufficient for email validation?
evidence: NOT REGEXP_LIKE finds violators; REGEXP_SUBSTR extracts

domains.name: Performance Tuning
domains.description: Execution plans, optimizer statistics, indexing strategy, and SQL optimization.

scenarios.title: Reading the plan
scenarios.situation: A report query suddenly runs 50x slower after a data load. The plan shows TABLE ACCESS FULL on a 10M-row table with E-Rows=100, A-Rows=10M.
scenarios.prompt: What does this tell you and what's first?
choices: The optimizer guessed 100 rows but got 10M — a cardinality misestimate, almost certainly stale statistics after the load. First step: gather stats on the table, then re-check the plan
Add an index immediately
Add a /*+ PARALLEL */ hint
Rewrite the query
scenarios.why: E-Rows vs A-Rows 100 vs 10M is the smoking gun: the optimizer planned for a trickle and got a flood. After a bulk load, statistics are the prime suspect — gather them before touching the query or adding indexes.
scenarios.hint: What does a huge E-Rows/A-Rows gap mean?
evidence: E-Rows << A-Rows after a load = stale stats; gather first

scenarios.title: Index or full scan?
scenarios.situation: Query: WHERE status = 'PENDING' on a 5M-row orders table; 95% of rows are 'SHIPPED', 5% 'PENDING'. There's no index on status.
choices: Partition the table by status
Add a function-based index on UPPER(status)
Create a B-tree index on status: 5% selectivity makes the index highly effective, and a histogram on the skewed column keeps the estimate honest
Full scan is fine — 5M rows is small
scenarios.why: 5% selectivity on 5M rows = 250K rows via index vs 5M via full scan — the B-tree wins clearly. The skewed distribution also wants a histogram so the optimizer believes the 5%.
scenarios.hint: At 5% selectivity, which access path wins and why?
evidence: Low-selectivity predicate + B-tree + histogram on skew

scenarios.title: Killing N+1
scenarios.situation: The orders page runs 1 query for 200 orders, then 200 queries for line items — 201 round trips, 4 seconds.
choices: Cache the page for 5 minutes
One JOIN (or a bulk fetch of line items for all 200 order IDs) — collapse 201 round trips into 1-2. The N+1 is a query-design problem, not a database-speed problem
Add an index on line_items.order_id
Increase the connection pool
scenarios.why: Round trips dominate: 200 sequential queries pay 200 network latencies. A single join returns the same data in one trip. Indexes help each query but don't fix the trip count; caching masks the design flaw.
scenarios.hint: What dominates N+1 latency — query speed or trip count?
evidence: N+1: collapse trips with a join/bulk fetch, not faster queries

scenarios.title: Slow loader
scenarios.situation: A PL/SQL loader inserts 2M rows with a FOR loop, one INSERT per row — 40 minutes.
choices: Add /*+ APPEND */ to the row-by-row INSERT
Run 10 copies of the loop in parallel
Disable all indexes permanently
BULK COLLECT with LIMIT 5000 in a loop + FORALL inserts — array fetching and array binding eliminate the per-row context switches; LIMIT keeps memory bounded
scenarios.why: The bottleneck is per-row SQL/PLSQL context switches — FORALL sends thousands of rows per round trip. APPEND helps but doesn't fix the loop; parallelism multiplies a bad pattern; dropping indexes permanently trades load speed for query speed.
scenarios.hint: What is the actual bottleneck in row-by-row loads?
evidence: BULK COLLECT LIMIT + FORALL = 10-100x on loads

scenarios.title: Function kills index
scenarios.situation: WHERE UPPER(email) = 'A@X.COM' does a full scan despite an index on email.
choices: Create a function-based index on UPPER(email) — the query's expression must match the index expression exactly, then the optimizer uses it
Drop the UPPER() and hope data is already upper
Add a hint /*+ INDEX(employees) */
Create a second plain index on email
scenarios.why: The index is on email, the predicate is on UPPER(email) — different expressions, no match. A function-based index on UPPER(email) gives the optimizer an access path for exactly this predicate. Hints can't conjure a matching index.
scenarios.hint: Why doesn't the plain index help this predicate?
evidence: Index the expression the query actually uses

scenarios.title: Plan flip after upgrade
scenarios.situation: After a DB upgrade, a critical query's plan flipped to a worse one. The query text can't change (packaged app).
choices: Gather stats with different settings until the plan flips back
SQL Plan Baseline capturing the known-good plan — baselines pin the good plan and only permit better ones, without touching the packaged SQL text
Add hints to the packaged app's queries
Downgrade the database
scenarios.why: Baselines are the production answer to plan instability: they enforce the proven plan regardless of optimizer version quirks, and they don't require editing vendor SQL. Hints need text changes; stat-fiddling is fragile.
scenarios.hint: Which mechanism pins a plan without editing SQL text?
evidence: SQL Plan Baselines > hints for packaged apps

scenarios.title: Covering index
scenarios.situation: Report: SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id runs every minute; the plan shows full table scan + hash group by on a 3M-row table.
choices: A bitmap index on department_id
Materialized view refreshed every minute
More PGA memory
A covering index on (department_id, salary) — the query's columns all live in the index, so the plan becomes an index fast full scan + group by, touching a fraction of the blocks
scenarios.why: The query needs only two narrow columns — a covering index serves them from compact index blocks instead of wide table blocks. Bitmap is wrong for OLTP; a per-minute MV refresh is heavier than the query; memory doesn't fix block volume.
scenarios.hint: When does an index eliminate the table access?
evidence: Covering index: all query columns in the index

domains.name: Transactions and Concurrency
domains.description: ACID, isolation levels, locking, undo/redo, and flashback technologies.

scenarios.title: Lost update
scenarios.situation: Two clerks open the same inventory row (stock=10), each sells 1, each writes stock=9. Final stock: 9, but 2 were sold.
choices: Pessimistic: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before modifying — the second clerk waits for the first's COMMIT and then sees stock=9, writing 8. Or optimistic: UPDATE ... WHERE version = v with retry
Increase the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE and hope
Run the updates at different times of day
Add a CHECK constraint on stock
scenarios.why: Read-modify-write without locking is the lost-update recipe: both read 10, both write 9. FOR UPDATE serializes the critical section; optimistic versioning detects the conflict at write time. Isolation level alone doesn't lock the row.
scenarios.hint: Why doesn't READ COMMITTED prevent this?
evidence: FOR UPDATE or version-guarded UPDATE on read-modify-write

scenarios.title: Deadlock in transfers
scenarios.situation: Transfer code locks the source account then the destination. Two concurrent transfers A->B and B->A deadlock with ORA-00060.
choices: Lock accounts in a consistent order (always the lower ID first) — both sessions then contend for the same first lock instead of deadlocking; the loser waits, no cycle
Catch ORA-00060 and retry forever
Run all transfers serially
Set a longer deadlock detection timeout
scenarios.why: Deadlocks need a lock-order cycle; consistent ordering (by ID) eliminates the cycle structurally — A->B and B->A both lock the lower ID first, so one waits cleanly. Retry-only still deadlocks under load; serial execution kills throughput.
scenarios.hint: What structural change eliminates the deadlock cycle?
evidence: Consistent lock ordering by key — no cycles, no deadlocks

scenarios.title: Work queue
scenarios.situation: Eight workers pull jobs from a jobs table. With plain SELECT FOR UPDATE, workers block each other and throughput collapses.
choices: Partition the table into 8 static chunks
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — each worker grabs the next unlocked row and skips rows other workers hold; no waiting, no double-processing
One worker at a time
SELECT FOR UPDATE NOWAIT with retry loops
scenarios.why: SKIP LOCKED is the queue primitive: contended rows are skipped, not waited on, so workers stay busy on disjoint rows. NOWAIT raises instead of skipping (retry storms); static chunks unbalance when jobs vary.
scenarios.hint: Which clause turns a table into a concurrent queue?
evidence: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — the work-queue primitive

scenarios.title: Bad update recovery
scenarios.situation: An UPDATE without WHERE set every salary to 5000 at 2 PM. It's 2:20 PM; the transaction committed. No backup restore allowed (too slow).
choices: Rebuild salaries from the HR spreadsheet
FLASHBACK DATABASE to 2 PM
Ask each employee their salary
Flashback Query: SELECT ... AS OF TIMESTAMP (2 PM minus a minute) to see pre-update values, then MERGE/UPDATE the table back from that snapshot — undo data is still within retention
scenarios.why: AS OF TIMESTAMP reads the pre-update image from undo — a targeted surgical restore of exactly the damaged column, no downtime, no full-database flashback. It works while undo retention covers the 20 minutes.
scenarios.hint: What lets you query the table as of 20 minutes ago?
evidence: AS OF TIMESTAMP — surgical recovery from undo

scenarios.title: Phantom report
scenarios.situation: A month-end report sums orders twice (start and end of the run); new orders committed mid-run make the two sums differ.
choices: SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY (or SERIALIZABLE) at the report's start — a consistent snapshot for the whole transaction; both sums read the same point in time
Lock the orders table for the report's duration
Run the report at 3 AM
Average the two sums
scenarios.why: READ COMMITTED gives statement-level consistency — each SELECT sees a new 'now'. A read-only transaction pins one snapshot for all statements, so repeated reads agree. Table locks block the business; 3 AM just hides the race.
scenarios.hint: Which level gives statement-vs-transaction consistency?
evidence: Reports needing repeatable reads: READ ONLY txn

scenarios.title: Partial batch failure
scenarios.situation: A 3-step nightly load: step 2 fails on bad data. Currently the whole load rolls back and steps 1's good work is lost, then everything reruns.
choices: SAVEPOINT after each step; on step-2 failure ROLLBACK TO the step-1 savepoint — keep step 1's work, fix the data, rerun from step 2. Idempotent steps make reruns safe
COMMIT after every row
Run each step in a separate database
Skip error handling — rerun everything
scenarios.why: Savepoints give surgical rollback: the failed step rewinds, completed steps survive. Per-row commits break atomicity and slow the load; separate databases don't fix the logic.
scenarios.hint: How do you keep step 1's work when step 2 fails?
evidence: SAVEPOINT per step; ROLLBACK TO on failure

scenarios.title: Snapshot too old
scenarios.situation: A 3-hour report fails with ORA-01555 snapshot too old. Undo retention is 15 minutes.
choices: Run the report twice and merge

Shorten the query (tune it under retention), enlarge undo + retention to cover the runtime, or run during low-DML windows — the query outlived its before-images; align retention with the longest consistent read
Add an index to make ORA-01555 go away
Restart the database
scenarios.why: ORA-01555 means the undo needed for the query's start-time snapshot aged out — the fix is retention >= longest query runtime, or a faster query. Indexes don't create undo; restarts don't either.
scenarios.hint: What does ORA-01555 actually mean?
evidence: Undo retention must exceed the longest consistent read

domains.name: Oracle Architecture
domains.description: Instance vs database, tablespaces, redo/undo, data dictionary, and multitenant architecture.

scenarios.title: SGA vs PGA
scenarios.situation: A junior says 'the SGA is per-user memory and the PGA is shared'.
choices: Both are shared equally
The distinction doesn't matter for tuning
Reversed: the SGA (buffer cache, shared pool) is shared across all sessions; the PGA is private per server process (sorts, hashes). Sizing the SGA affects everyone; PGA pressure shows per-session
They're right — SGA is per-user
scenarios.why: Shared vs private is the fundamental split: one SGA serves the instance; each session gets its own PGA. Tuning advice flips completely depending on which is pressured — shared-pool contention vs per-session sort spills.
scenarios.hint: Which memory is shared across sessions?
evidence: SGA = shared (buffer cache, shared pool); PGA = per-process

scenarios.title: Startup stages
scenarios.situation: The database won't open. Alert log shows the control file is missing.
scenarios.prompt: At which startup stage does it fail, and what's the implication?
choices: OPEN — datafiles are the problem
SHUTDOWN — it never started
MOUNT — the instance started (NOMOUNT OK) but can't find the control file to mount; restore the control file from multiplexed copies or backup before OPEN is possible
NOMOUNT — the instance can't start
scenarios.why: NOMOUNT needs only the instance; MOUNT reads the control file; OPEN opens datafiles. Control-file loss fails at MOUNT — multiplexed copies or a backup restore fix it; datafiles aren't even attempted yet.
scenarios.hint: What does each startup stage require?

scenarios.title: Recovery posture
scenarios.situation: A production database is in NOARCHIVELOG mode. The manager says 'backups run nightly, we're fine'.
choices: Not fine: NOARCHIVELOG means any failure loses everything since the last cold backup — no point-in-time recovery, no hot backups. Production requires ARCHIVELOG + archived-redo retention
Agree — nightly backups are enough
Switch to weekly backups instead
Disable backups to save space
scenarios.why: ARCHIVELOG is what makes recovery complete: archived redo bridges the gap between the last backup and the failure point. Nightly cold backups in NOARCHIVELOG cap your recovery at 'last night, with downtime'.
scenarios.hint: What does ARCHIVELOG enable that nightly backups don't?
evidence: Production = ARCHIVELOG; NOARCHIVELOG = accept data loss

scenarios.title: SYSTEM full
scenarios.situation: Monitoring alerts: SYSTEM tablespace 98% full. A developer created large tables there 'temporarily'.
choices: Drop the data dictionary tables to free space
Ignore — 98% is fine
Move the user objects out of SYSTEM/SYSAUX into a proper tablespace immediately — the data dictionary lives there and a full SYSTEM can halt the database; then set up alerting and quota discipline
Add a datafile to SYSTEM and leave the tables
scenarios.why: SYSTEM/SYSAUX are Oracle's home — user objects there risk dictionary operations failing when space exhausts. The fix is relocation, not expansion: adding space to SYSTEM normalizes the violation.
scenarios.hint: Why must user data never live in SYSTEM?
evidence: SYSTEM/SYSAUX = Oracle only; user data gets its own tablespaces

scenarios.title: Finding blockers
scenarios.situation: Users report hangs. You suspect a blocking lock.
choices: Wait for the hang to clear
Query V$LOCK joined to V$SESSION for block=1/request>0 — identifies the blocker session and the waiters in one query; then check what SQL the blocker runs in V$SQL
Restart the database
Kill all sessions
scenarios.why: V$ views are the live X-ray: the blocker/waiter join names the exact sessions, and V$SQL shows the offending statement. Restarts and mass-kills treat the symptom blindly and disrupt everyone.
scenarios.hint: Which views expose live blocking chains?
evidence: V$LOCK + V$SESSION + V$SQL — the blocking triad

scenarios.title: Where's my data?
scenarios.situation: You create a table while connected to the CDB root, then can't see it from the PDB service.
choices: The table needs 10 minutes to replicate
PDBs share all objects with the root
You need a database link
Objects created in CDB$ROOT belong to the root container — PDBs are separate namespaces. Reconnect to the PDB service and create it there; user data never belongs in the root
scenarios.why: Containers are namespaces: root objects are invisible to PDBs by design. The fix is connecting to the right container (PDB service name), not replication or links.
scenarios.hint: Which container should hold user data?
evidence: User data in PDBs; CDB$ROOT is Oracle's

scenarios.title: Excessive grant
scenarios.situation: A developer asks for the DBA role on production 'to make the app work'.
choices: Grant DBA — it's faster
Grant DBA temporarily and forget to revoke
Give them the SYS password instead

Refuse and grant least privilege: diagnose the actual missing privilege (usually CREATE SESSION + specific object grants), grant exactly that, document it. DBA 'to make it work' is a security incident waiting to happen
scenarios.why: Least privilege is non-negotiable on production: the DBA role can drop the database. The professional move is diagnosing the real requirement and granting precisely it — five minutes of diagnosis beats a breach.
scenarios.hint: What does least privilege require here?
evidence: Diagnose the missing privilege; never grant DBA for convenience

domains.name: SQL Exam Prep
domains.description: Oracle SQL certification exam strategy: question patterns, trap recognition, and timed practice.

scenarios.title: Question triage
scenarios.situation: The SQL exam opens. 60 questions, 90 minutes. First question is a 40-line query asking for the 3rd bug.
choices: Guess immediately to save time
Read all 60 questions first, then start
Flag it and move on — bank the quick wins first (single-concept questions), then return with remaining time. Per-question budget is 90 seconds; a 5-minute opener starves ten later questions
Solve it now — question 1 sets the tone
scenarios.why: Triage beats heroics: easy questions carry the same marks as hard ones, and time is the binding constraint. Flag-and-return converts a time-sink into a second-pass problem with fresh eyes.
scenarios.hint: What's the per-question budget and what does it imply?
evidence: 90s/question; flag time-sinks, harvest easy marks first

scenarios.title: NULL trap question
scenarios.situation: Stem: 'Which query returns employees with no manager?' Options include WHERE manager_id = NULL, WHERE manager_id != 0, WHERE manager_id IS NULL, WHERE NVL(manager_id,0) = 0.
scenarios.prompt: Correct pick and why the distractors fail?
choices: WHERE manager_id != 0
WHERE NVL(manager_id, 0) = 0
IS NULL — = NULL is never true (UNKNOWN), != 0 excludes NULLs too (comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN), NVL works but is the slower non-idiomatic form the exam doesn't reward
WHERE manager_id = NULL
scenarios.why: NULL is not a value — every comparison with it yields UNKNOWN, which filters the row out. = NULL and != 0 both silently return nothing; IS NULL is the direct test. NVL works but the exam rewards the idiom.
scenarios.hint: What does any comparison with NULL return?
evidence: Any comparison with NULL = UNKNOWN = filtered out

scenarios.title: GROUP BY trap
scenarios.situation: Stem shows SELECT department_id, last_name, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY department_id and asks what happens.
choices: It returns one row per employee
It returns NULL for last_name
ORA-00979 not a GROUP BY expression — last_name is neither grouped nor aggregated; Oracle enforces this strictly. Fix: add it to GROUP BY or aggregate it
It runs fine — Oracle picks a last_name
scenarios.why: Oracle has no loose-grouping mode: every SELECT item must be functionally dependent on the GROUP BY or aggregated. The error is the answer — and recognizing ORA-00979 by sight saves minutes.
scenarios.hint: Which error does a bare non-aggregated column raise?
evidence: ORA-00979: not a GROUP BY expression

scenarios.title: ROWNUM trap
scenarios.situation: Stem: 'Return the 5 highest-paid employees.' Options include WHERE ROWNUM <= 5 ORDER BY salary DESC, subquery with ORDER BY then ROWNUM filter, FETCH FIRST 5, and RANK() approaches.
choices: The subquery (ORDER BY inside, ROWNUM outside), FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY, and the RANK() variant — all sort before limiting. The bare WHERE ROWNUM <= 5 ORDER BY is wrong: ROWNUM assigns before sorting
WHERE ROWNUM <= 5 ORDER BY salary DESC
ORDER BY salary DESC WHERE ROWNUM <= 5
ROWNUM < 5 without ORDER BY
scenarios.why: ROWNUM is assigned as rows are fetched — before ORDER BY. Correct patterns all share one property: sort first, limit second (subquery wrap, FETCH FIRST, or analytic). The wrong option is the exam's favorite trap.
scenarios.hint: When is ROWNUM assigned relative to ORDER BY?
evidence: Assigned before sort — wrap the ORDER BY in a subquery

scenarios.title: Join elimination
scenarios.situation: Stem: 'List all employees and their department names, including employees without departments.'
choices: INNER JOIN
RIGHT JOIN
CROSS JOIN
LEFT JOIN departments — preserves all employees, NULLs where no match. INNER would drop the department-less; RIGHT/FULL answer different questions
scenarios.why: 'Including X without Y' is the LEFT JOIN trigger phrase: the left table is fully preserved. INNER silently drops the very rows the question asks about — the classic one-word-that-changes-everything stem.
scenarios.hint: Which phrase in the stem dictates the join type?

scenarios.title: Constraint question
scenarios.situation: Stem: 'Ensure every order references an existing customer, and deleting a customer is blocked while orders exist.'
choices: UNIQUE constraint on customer_id
A trigger that deletes the orders too
FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id) with the default NO ACTION — the FK guarantees referential integrity; default behavior blocks the parent delete while children exist
CHECK constraint on customer_id
scenarios.why: Referential integrity is the FOREIGN KEY's job; the default (NO ACTION/RESTRICT) blocks parent deletion with dependent rows. CHECK validates values, not existence; the trigger describes CASCADE, the opposite of what's asked.
scenarios.hint: Which constraint enforces 'references an existing row'?

scenarios.title: Educated guessing
scenarios.situation: Five questions remain, 3 minutes left. Each has 4 options; no penalty for wrong answers.
choices: Leave them blank — wrong answers feel worse
Guess randomly without reading
Spend all 3 minutes on one question
Answer every one — eliminate obviously wrong options first (NULL traps, ROWNUM-before-sort), then guess among the rest. Blanks score zero; a supported guess has positive expected value
scenarios.why: No-penalty scoring makes blanks strictly dominated: even a pure guess has 25% expected value vs 0. Thirty seconds of elimination per question (kill the trap options) pushes that well above 25%.
scenarios.hint: What's the expected value of a blank vs a guess?
evidence: No penalty: eliminate, then guess — never blank

lessons.title: SELECT Deep Dive — Core concepts
concepts: Group functions: SQL evaluates in logical order: FROM → WHERE (row filter) → GROUP BY → HAVING (group filter) → SELECT → ORDER BY. Logical evaluation order strikes again: WHERE and GROUP BY execute before the SELECT list, so aliases don't exist yet; ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so aliases are visible.
Aggregate functions: all aggregate functions except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs. To get one row per last name, aggregate (GROUP BY last_name) or use a subquery/window function to pick a representative row.

NULL handling: oracle treats NULL as the largest value for sorting: ASC puts NULLs last, DESC puts NULLs first — by default. COUNT(*) = 107 rows; COUNT(commission_pct) = 35 non-NULL commissions, so 72 employees have NULL commission_pct.
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows across the full select list — 'Smith, John' vs 'Smith, Jane' are different rows, so both survive.

example.code:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS c
FROM employees
WHERE COUNT(*) > 10
GROUP BY dept_id;
example.walkthrough: SQL evaluates in logical order: FROM → WHERE (row filter) → GROUP BY → HAVING (group filter) → SELECT → ORDER BY. Aggregates don't exist yet at WHERE time, hence ORA-00934. The fix: GROUP BY dept_id then HAVING COUNT(*) > 10.

pitfalls: Common trap: WHERE can reference aggregate functions in Oracle if placed after GROUP BY.
Common trap: ORDER BY is ignored with ROWNUM; sorting is impossible in Oracle.
Common trap: oracle sorts NULLs first in ascending order by default.
Common trap: the ORDER BY is fine; NULLs indicate missing rows, not missing values.

lessons.title: Joins & Subqueries — Core concepts
concepts: NULL in joins: a self join gives the table two aliases (e for employee, m for manager) and joins e.manager_id = m.employee_id. NULL never equals anything, including NULL — so equality join conditions exclude NULL keys on both sides.
INNER vs LEFT JOIN: LEFT JOIN keeps all employees (NULL department shows as NULL). It runs per row (fine for small sets; a LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY scales better for large ones).

EXISTS vs IN: NOT EXISTS uses a correlated predicate that stays NULL-safe, and EXISTS short-circuits on first match — also why EXISTS often outperforms IN on large sets. Correlated = per-row context; the trade-off is repeated execution, which is why EXISTS (short-circuit) often beats IN here.
NOT IN NULL trap: this is the same reason NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns no rows: the anti-join predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN.

Correlated subqueries: a scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column per outer row — correlated here to compute per-department headcount. A correlated subquery references the outer query's row (e.department_id), so it re-evaluates per row with that row's department — giving a per-department average.

example.code:
SELECT last_name FROM employees
WHERE department_id NOT IN (SELECT department_id FROM departments);
example.walkthrough: NOT IN (list with NULL) → for each row, department_id NOT IN (…, NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN (because x <> NULL is UNKNOWN), and WHERE keeps only TRUE. NOT EXISTS uses a correlated predicate that stays NULL-safe, and EXISTS short-circuits on first match — also why EXISTS often outperforms IN on large sets.

pitfalls: Common trap: INNER JOIN treats NULL as equal to NULL.
Common trap: NULL department_id joins to every department with NULL id.
Common trap: the join will error on NULL keys.
Common trap: self joins are not allowed in Oracle.
