lessons.title: DDL/DML & Constraints — Core concepts
concepts: Foreign keys: AS IDENTITY) for surrogate keys, or a trigger. The rule: sequences for keys, custom logic for gapless documents.

TRUNCATE vs DELETE: choose TRUNCATE for full-table resets, DELETE when you need selectivity, triggers, or transactional control. MERGE also supports DELETE clauses and is the standard upsert in Oracle.
DDL vs DML: TRUNCATE TABLE is DDL: it drops storage segments (fast, resets the high-water mark), issues an implicit commit, fires no row triggers, and can't be rolled back statement-by-statement.
CHECK constraints: legit fixes: insert parent first (normal flow), or define the constraint DEFERRABLE and SET CONSTRAINTS DEFERRED to validate at commit.

Constraint states: fixes: DEFAULT ON NULL (12c+, treats explicit NULL as 'use default'), a NOT NULL constraint to reject it, an identity column (GENERATED ... ADD CONSTRAINT validates all existing rows by default.

example.code:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_cust
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id);
example.walkthrough: A foreign key enforces that every child value exists in the parent key — the child can't precede the parent. Disabling the FK destroys the guarantee; Oracle never auto-creates parents.

pitfalls: Common trap: foreign keys only validate on SELECT, so the error is elsewhere.
Common trap: TRUNCATE and DELETE are identical except speed.
Common trap: use a CHECK constraint to convert NULLs.
Common trap: DEFAULT applies to explicit NULLs too; the app is wrong.

lessons.title: Functions — Core concepts
concepts: NVL: for fallback chains or expensive defaults, COALESCE is the correct tool; NVL is fine for simple two-value defaults.
COALESCE (ANSI standard) evaluates left-to-right and stops at the first non-NULL, and takes N arguments.
NULL handling: CASE (simple and searched forms) is ANSI, supports any condition (ranges, NULL checks, compound predicates), and nests cleanly.

Date arithmetic: for date math: ADD_MONTHS(date, n) handles month-end correctly (Jan 31 + 1 month = Feb 28/29). Explicit TO_DATE('2026-10-03','YYYY-MM-DD') or ANSI DATE '2026-10-03' literals are deterministic.
MONTHS_BETWEEN = fractional months.

example.code:
SELECT NVL(expensive_fn(x), 0) FROM t;  -- slow even when x is not null
SELECT COALESCE(x, expensive_fn(y), 0) FROM t;  -- fast
example.walkthrough: NVL always evaluates both arguments — no short-circuit — and requires compatible types. COALESCE (ANSI standard) evaluates left-to-right and stops at the first non-NULL, and takes N arguments.

pitfalls: Common trap: SUBSTR alone with fixed positions.
Common trap: TO_DATE on an already-date value to 'normalize' it.
Common trap: subtracting dates gives months in Oracle.
Common trap: implicit conversion is fine; NLS_DATE_FORMAT is always 'YYYY-MM-DD'.
lessons.try_it: Try it now in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: PL/SQL Blocks — Core concepts
concepts: SELECT INTO requires exactly one row: zero rows → NO_DATA_FOUND (ORA-01403), multiple → TOO_MANY_ROWS.
Exception handling: without an EXCEPTION handler, the error propagates up, aborting the block and rolling back uncommitted work to the last COMMIT.
%TYPE binds a variable's datatype to a table column; %ROWTYPE binds a record to a whole row.
BULK COLLECT fetches batches into collections; FORALL sends DML as array operations — one switch per batch.

example.walkthrough: %TYPE binds a variable's datatype to a table column; %ROWTYPE binds a record to a whole row. Schema changes propagate automatically — no code edits, no truncation bugs. Hardcoded types create a hidden contract with the DDL that breaks silently.

pitfalls: Common trap: implicit cursors can't be used with SELECT.
Common trap: use a cursor FOR loop with an inner SELECT per row.
Common trap: SELECT INTO returns NULL when no rows match.
Common trap: %TYPE is documentation only; it doesn't affect the datatype.
lessons.try_it: Try it now in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Packages & Triggers — Core concepts
concepts: Packages also group related logic, support overloading, and hold session-persistent state. Guidance: keep triggers for auditing, simple validation/defaulting, and enforcing invariants close to data; put business workflows in named, explicitly-called procedures/packages.
Spec vs body: the spec is the contract: public procedures, types, constants.

Trigger timing: the sanctioned pattern: compound trigger — collect :NEW keys in the row section, query/process in the AFTER STATEMENT section when the table is stable. Granularity + timing must match the job.
Row vs statement: statement-level triggers fire once per statement and can't see row values.
Mutating table error: during row-level trigger execution the table is 'mutating' — mid-DML, in an inconsistent state — so Oracle forbids querying it (prevents seeing partial changes).
Compound triggers: triggers fire implicitly — invisible at the call site — making behavior surprising and hard to debug, with ordering and recursion hazards.

example.code:
ALTER PROCEDURE calc_bonus COMPILE; -- succeeds
-- but 4 views and 2 triggers are now INVALID
example.walkthrough: Oracle tracks dependencies: changing a procedure's signature invalidates dependents. They auto-recompile on next access, but a runtime recompile failure becomes a production error — so deployments should explicitly recompile and verify (UTL_RECOMP, DBMS_UTILITY.COMPILE_SCHEMA) and check for INVALID objects. Signature changes are breaking changes; body-only changes via package bodies avoid invalidation.

pitfalls: Common trap: invalid objects fix themselves instantly with no risk.
Common trap: package variables reset after every statement.
Common trap: the body is public and the spec is private.
Common trap: INSTEAD OF trigger on the base table.
lessons.try_it: Try it now in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Oracle SQL - Core concepts
concepts: SQL executes in a fixed order: FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after - putting an aggregate in WHERE is the ORA-00934 everyone meets once.

Joins multiply rows before filtering, so always write the join condition; a missing ON turns an inner join into a Cartesian product. NULL never equals NULL, so gaps found by outer joins need IS NULL checks.
GROUP BY collapses rows: every selected column must be grouped or aggregated. Reach for HAVING when the filter depends on the aggregate itself.

Analytic functions compute over a window without collapsing rows: OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) restarts the calculation per group. ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD, and running SUM() cover most reporting needs.

Subqueries and CTEs (WITH) structure complex logic; correlated subqueries execute per outer row, so prefer set-based rewrites when they dominate runtime. NOT IN is dangerous when the subquery can return NULL - NOT EXISTS is the safe form.
DDL is a contract: primary and foreign keys, NOT NULL, CHECK, and UNIQUE constraints protect data quality at the source. Indexes speed reads but tax writes, so index for the queries you actually run.

example.walkthrough: The analytic SUM keeps one row per employee while accumulating salary within each department in hire-date order. A GROUP BY version would collapse to one row per department and lose the per-employee detail the report needs.

pitfalls: Common trap: = NULL - it never matches; use IS NULL.
Common trap: ROWNUM with ORDER BY at the same query level - ROWNUM is assigned before sorting; nest the ordered query inside.
Common trap: SELECT * in views and application code - a schema change silently shifts column positions; name your columns.
Common trap: forgetting ORDER BY inside OVER() - running totals and rankings become nondeterministic.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Oracle Sql move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of SELECT Deep Dive
concepts: SELECT Deep Dive is a multi-step process within SELECT Deep Dive: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect SELECT Deep Dive to the broader SELECT Deep Dive ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  SELECT Deep Dive begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: This bootcamp has 15 domains: 6 core SQL domains, 5 advanced domains, plus start-here, capstone, mock assessment, and exam prep. Work them in order — SELECT before joins, joins before PL/SQL.

Lessons teach concepts with runnable SQL examples; scenarios test query judgment under realistic stems; labs give hands-on reps against a practice schema. The mock assessment pulls scenarios from every domain under time pressure.
The Oracle SQL exam tests whether you can read and write correct SQL, not recite definitions. Every scenario is a mini query decision — practice choosing the right construct with trade-offs.
Track readiness per domain: 80%+ on scenario sets before moving on. The exam-prep domain loops back to weak areas — plan for two passes, not one.

example.code: Week 1: start-here + SELECT + joins. Week 2: DDL/DML + functions + PL/SQL. Week 3: advanced queries + tuning + capstone. Week 4: exam-prep + mocks to 85%+.
example.walkthrough: Your 4-week arc: foundations, programming, advanced, then prove it.

pitfalls: Skipping SELECT fundamentals — everything assumes them.
Reading without running the SQL — execute every example.
One pass instead of two.

lessons.title: Study Strategy for the Oracle SQL Exam
concepts: The exam blueprint weights: SELECT/joins/subqueries heaviest, then DDL/DML, single-row functions, and PL/SQL basics. Study proportionally — SELECT semantics are nearly half the exam.
Learn in dependency order: SELECT -> joins -> subqueries -> DDL/DML -> functions -> PL/SQL. Each layer's questions assume the previous layer's constructs.
For every construct, know: what it's for, the exact syntax, one common trap, and when to choose it over the alternative. 'Which query returns X' is the exam's favorite shape.
Build a personal 'trap list' as you go: one line per gotcha (NULL behavior, ROWNUM ordering, GROUP BY rules). Review it daily in week 4 — it's your whole exam on one page.

example.code: Trap list line: 'NOT IN + NULL in list = zero rows; use NOT EXISTS.' One line per trap, reviewed daily.

pitfalls: Studying alphabetically instead of by blueprint weight.
Memorizing syntax without the trap patterns.

lessons.title: Course Roadmap Overview
concepts: Core domains (1-6): SELECT, joins/subqueries, DDL/DML, functions, PL/SQL blocks, packages/triggers — the working SQL programmer's toolkit. These six are the exam's center of gravity.
Advanced domains (7-11): advanced queries, performance tuning, transactions/concurrency, Oracle architecture, plus exam-prep — the specialist layer, and the capstone that proves you can build.
Capstone: design and build an analytics mart — schema, ETL loads, reporting queries, tuned and documented. It's the portfolio piece — 'I built this' beats 'I studied this'.
Systems-anatomy runs alongside as your reference layer for how SQL maps to the engine. Consult it whenever execution behavior confuses you.

lessons.title: Terminal and Lab Guide for SQL
concepts: Labs run against a practice Oracle schema (HR-like) via SQL*Plus or SQL Developer. The pattern: connect, run, verify row counts, disconnect. Every lab states its schema and stop conditions.
Connection: sqlplus hr/hr@localhost:1521/XEPDB1 (practice credentials). Never run untested DML without a WHERE check — SELECT first with the same predicate, then UPDATE/DELETE.
Lab hygiene: wrap destructive practice in transactions (ROLLBACK to undo), verify with SELECT after each DML, and COMMIT only when the lab says so. Uncommitted experiments vanish safely.
Execution order is your debugger: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY. When a query surprises you, trace it in execution order, not written order.

example.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees;
-- 107 rows: the practice schema is loaded and ready
example.walkthrough: Count the rows first — know your data before querying it.

pitfalls: DML without a WHERE check.
COMMIT on experimental changes.
Tracing queries in written order.

lessons.title: Phase 1: Schema Design
concepts: The capstone builds an analytics mart: a star schema (fact_orders, dim_customer, dim_product, dim_date) loaded from a transactional source. Phase 1 designs the schema with constraints, indexes, and documentation.
Design decisions: surrogate keys (identity columns) vs natural keys, slowly-changing-dimension strategy (type 1 overwrite for this build), partition the fact table by month for manageability.
Constraints as documentation: PKs, FKs, NOT NULLs, CHECKs — the schema enforces its own integrity. Name every constraint; the data dictionary becomes the spec.
Deliverable: DDL scripts, an ER diagram, and a one-page design rationale (grain statement, key choices, partition strategy). Reviewed before any data loads.

example.walkthrough: Surrogate key, natural-key unique constraint — the dimension pattern.

pitfalls: No grain statement — 'what is one row?' unanswered.
Natural keys as primary keys in dimensions.
Unnamed constraints.
lessons.try_it: Write the grain statement for fact_orders

lessons.title: Phase 2: ETL and Loading
concepts: Phase 2 loads the mart: extract from the source schema, transform (cleanse, conform, surrogate-key lookup), load with bulk operations. BULK COLLECT + FORALL for the row processing; MERGE for the dimension upserts.
Load pattern: stage tables first (raw source snapshot), then transform into dimensions (MERGE for SCD1), then facts (bulk insert with key lookups). Staging makes reruns safe and debuggable.
Data quality: validate row counts at each step (source -> stage -> mart), log rejected rows with reasons, and make the load idempotent (rerunnable without duplication).
Scheduling: the load runs nightly via DBMS_SCHEDULER; each run logs start/end/rowcounts to a control table. Operational ETL is observable ETL.

example.code:
MERGE INTO dim_customer d USING stage_customer s
ON (d.customer_id = s.customer_id)
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET d.customer_name = s.customer_name
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (customer_id, customer_name, region)
VALUES (s.customer_id, s.customer_name, s.region);
example.walkthrough: MERGE handles the SCD1 upsert — one statement, both cases.

pitfalls: Direct source-to-mart loads without staging.
Row-by-row inserts for 1M rows.
No rowcount validation between steps.
lessons.try_it: Design the stage -> dimension -> fact flow

lessons.title: Phase 3: Queries, Tuning, and Delivery
concepts: Phase 3 delivers the analytics: 10 reporting queries (KPIs, trends, top-N, YoY), each tuned (explain plan reviewed, indexes added where justified) and documented with business purpose.
Tuning loop: write the query, EXPLAIN PLAN, fix the worst operation (missing index, bad join order), re-measure. Document the before/after — the tuning log is a deliverable.
Views and materialized views: expose clean interfaces (views for logic, MVs for expensive aggregates). The mart's consumers query the views, never the raw facts.
Deliverable: query library with plans, a performance summary, and a 5-minute demo (question -> query -> answer). Present it like an analytics review — because that's the job.

example.code:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_monthly_sales
REFRESH COMPLETE ON DEMAND AS
SELECT TRUNC(order_date,'MM') m, SUM(amount) total
FROM fact_orders GROUP BY TRUNC(order_date,'MM');
example.walkthrough: Monthly sales pre-aggregated — the dashboard query becomes instant.

pitfalls: Untuned queries in the deliverable.
Consumers querying raw fact tables.
No before/after tuning documentation.
lessons.try_it: Write and tune your first KPI query

lessons.title: WHERE: Filtering Rows Correctly
concepts: WHERE filters rows before any grouping or SELECT projection — it cannot reference column aliases defined in SELECT. 'WHERE total > 100' fails when total is an alias; repeat the expression or filter later.
NULL is never equal to anything, including NULL: WHERE manager_id = NULL returns zero rows, always. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL. This single rule explains a third of wrong-row bugs.
BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends; LIKE patterns use % (any string) and _ (one char). Escape literal wildcards with ESCAPE when searching for '100%'.

IN vs EXISTS vs JOIN for membership tests: IN with a NULL in the list returns UNKNOWN for non-matches (rows vanish); NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery returns zero rows — the classic disappearing-rows bug.

example.code:
-- the vanishing rows bug
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE department_id NOT IN (SELECT department_id FROM departments);
-- if the subquery returns even one NULL, this returns NOTHING
example.walkthrough: NOT IN + NULL = empty result. Rewrite as NOT EXISTS or filter NULLs from the subquery.

pitfalls: = NULL instead of IS NULL.
NOT IN over a subquery that can return NULL.
Referencing a SELECT alias in WHERE.
lessons.try_it: Predict: NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns what?

lessons.title: ORDER BY, FETCH, and Pagination
concepts: ORDER BY runs after SELECT — it CAN use aliases. Sort keys: ORDER BY salary DESC, hire_date; NULLS FIRST/LAST controls NULL placement (Oracle defaults NULLS LAST for ASC).
FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY (12c+) replaces the old ROWNUM dance for top-N. ROWNUM is assigned before ORDER BY — 'WHERE ROWNUM <= 5 ORDER BY salary DESC' returns 5 random rows sorted, not the top 5.
Pagination: OFFSET m ROWS FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY. Deep offsets get slow (the engine still reads the skipped rows) — keyset pagination (WHERE id > last_seen) scales better for infinite scroll.
Top-N per group needs window functions (ROW_NUMBER), not FETCH — FETCH limits the whole result, not each group.

example.walkthrough: ROWNUM is assigned as rows are read, before sorting. FETCH applies after ORDER BY.

pitfalls: ROWNUM with ORDER BY expecting top-N.
OFFSET pagination on million-row tables.
FETCH FIRST expecting per-group top-N.
lessons.try_it: Write top-3 earners per department two ways

lessons.title: DISTINCT, Aggregates, and GROUP BY
concepts: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows across the whole SELECT list; DISTINCT on one column of many still compares full rows. COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values.
GROUP BY collapses rows per group; every SELECT item must be grouped or aggregated — Oracle enforces this strictly (no MySQL-style loose grouping).
HAVING filters groups after aggregation; WHERE filters rows before. 'Departments with more than 5 employees' is HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 — WHERE cannot see the count.
NULL groups: GROUP BY puts all NULL keys in one group. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs — the two differ exactly by the NULL count in that column.

example.code:
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC;
example.walkthrough: Read it in execution order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY.

pitfalls: Non-aggregated, non-grouped column in SELECT.
WHERE on an aggregate ('WHERE COUNT(*) > 5').
COUNT(col) when COUNT(*) was meant.
lessons.try_it: Write: departments with avg salary > 8000

lessons.title: CASE Expressions and Conditional Logic
concepts: CASE is SQL's if-then: searched CASE (WHEN condition THEN value) or simple CASE (CASE col WHEN val). It returns one value per row — use it in SELECT, ORDER BY, even GROUP BY.
Bucketing pattern: CASE WHEN salary < 5000 THEN 'junior' WHEN salary < 10000 THEN 'mid' ELSE 'senior' END groups rows into bands you can then aggregate — conditional aggregation.
Conditional aggregates: SUM(CASE WHEN department_id = 50 THEN salary END) totals one department's pay in a single pass — pivoting without PIVOT.
COALESCE(a, b, c) returns the first non-NULL; NVL(a, b) is Oracle's two-arg version. Use them to tame NULLs in arithmetic — NULL + anything = NULL.

example.code:
SELECT CASE WHEN salary < 5000 THEN 'junior'
              WHEN salary < 10000 THEN 'mid'
              ELSE 'senior' END AS band,
       COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM employees GROUP BY CASE WHEN salary < 5000 THEN 'junior'
              WHEN salary < 10000 THEN 'mid' ELSE 'senior' END;
example.walkthrough: The same CASE in SELECT and GROUP BY — the bucket is computed, then aggregated.

pitfalls: Forgetting ELSE — unmatched rows become NULL silently.
CASE in WHERE written as a value instead of a boolean.
NULL arithmetic without COALESCE/NVL.
lessons.try_it: Bucket employees into 3 salary bands with counts

lessons.title: Join Types and Their Row Semantics
concepts: INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows; LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows with NULLs for missing right matches; FULL OUTER keeps both sides' orphans. Draw the Venn diagram, then write the join.

CROSS JOIN is every combination (m x n rows) — rarely intended; an accidental cross join from a missing ON clause explodes row counts. If the row count multiplies unexpectedly, check the join condition.
USING (col) vs ON: USING merges the join column into one output column; ON keeps both (employees.department_id and departments.department_id). Prefer ON for clarity in multi-table joins.
Join order does not change the result for inner joins (the optimizer reorders), but it changes readability: start from the driving table and walk the relationships.

example.code:
SELECT e.first_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
-- every employee, even those with no department (NULL name)
example.walkthrough: LEFT JOIN answers 'all X, plus their Y if any' — the most common reporting join.

pitfalls: Missing ON clause -> accidental cross join.
INNER JOIN when the question says 'including those with none'.
USING then referencing the ambiguous merged column wrong.
lessons.try_it: Write: all departments with employee counts (incl. empty)

lessons.title: Multi-Table Joins and Self Joins
concepts: Chain joins through the relationship path: employees -> departments -> locations. Each hop needs its own ON; a 4-table join has 3 join conditions — count them.
Self join: the same table twice with different aliases — employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id gives 'employee and their manager'. Aliases are mandatory, not cosmetic.
Fan-out: joining a one-to-many-to-many path multiplies rows (employee x orders x items). Aggregates after fan-out double-count — aggregate before joining, or use COUNT(DISTINCT).
Filter placement: conditions on the preserved table go in WHERE; conditions on the optional side of an outer join go in ON — WHERE on the optional side converts the outer join to an inner one.

example.code:
-- employee -> manager self join
SELECT e.first_name AS emp, m.first_name AS mgr
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;
example.walkthrough: Same table, two roles: e is the employee, m is the manager. The alias IS the role.

pitfalls: WHERE on the nullable side of a LEFT JOIN (kills the outer).
Aggregating after a fan-out join.
Self join without aliases — 'ambiguous column'.
lessons.try_it: Write: employees and their managers' departments

lessons.title: Subqueries: Scalar, Row, and Table
concepts: Scalar subquery returns one value: WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees). It must return exactly one row — more rows is an error, zero rows is NULL.
IN / ANY / ALL compare against a list: = ANY is IN; > ALL means 'greater than every value'. Correlated subqueries reference the outer query and re-run per row — powerful, potentially slow.
EXISTS checks presence without returning data: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ...) — stops at the first match, NULL-safe, usually the fastest membership test.
Derived tables (subquery in FROM) must be aliased: FROM (SELECT ...) t. They let you aggregate-then-join, defeating fan-out by collapsing before the join.

example.code:
-- departments with above-average headcount
SELECT d.department_name
FROM departments d
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e
       WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id)
      > (SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) cnt FROM employees GROUP BY department_id));
example.walkthrough: Correlated subquery per department vs the overall average — read inside-out.

pitfalls: Scalar subquery returning multiple rows.
NOT IN with NULLs (again — use NOT EXISTS).
Derived table without an alias.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite a NOT IN as NOT EXISTS

lessons.title: WITH Clauses (CTEs) and Readability
concepts: WITH names a subquery once and references it like a table: WITH dept_avg AS (SELECT ...). Complex queries become readable pipelines — each CTE is one thought.
CTEs chain: later CTEs reference earlier ones. 'Top departments, then their employees' is two CTEs, not one monster query. Readability is correctness — you cannot debug what you cannot read.
Recursive CTEs (WITH ... CONNECT BY is Oracle's native syntax for hierarchies): employee -> manager chains, org charts, bill-of-materials. START WITH the root, CONNECT BY the parent link.

CONNECT BY specifics: PRIOR marks the parent side; LEVEL gives depth; NOCYCLE prevents infinite loops on bad data. 'Org chart with levels' is START WITH manager_id IS NULL CONNECT BY PRIOR employee_id = manager_id.

example.code:
SELECT LEVEL, first_name, last_name
FROM employees
START WITH manager_id IS NULL
CONNECT BY PRIOR employee_id = manager_id
ORDER SIBLINGS BY first_name;
example.walkthrough: PRIOR employee_id = manager_id: the parent's id matches the child's manager — the hierarchy walks itself.

pitfalls: PRIOR on the wrong side — hierarchy walks downward instead of up.
No NOCYCLE on dirty hierarchy data — infinite loop.
One 80-line query instead of chained CTEs.
lessons.try_it: Write the org chart with LEVEL for your schema

lessons.title: Set Operators: UNION, INTERSECT, MINUS
concepts: UNION stacks result sets (deduped); UNION ALL keeps duplicates (faster — no sort). INTERSECT keeps common rows; MINUS keeps rows in the first but not the second. Column counts and types must align.
UNION vs UNION ALL is a performance decision: dedup costs a sort. Use ALL unless the question needs distinct rows — exams test this cost awareness.
MINUS answers 'in A but not B': employees with no department, products never ordered. It is the set-operator form of NOT EXISTS — often clearer for 'missing' questions.
Each branch can have its own WHERE/GROUP BY; ORDER BY goes once at the very end and references the first branch's column names or positions.

example.code:
-- employees in no department's location set
SELECT employee_id FROM employees
MINUS
SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
example.walkthrough: MINUS reads as the question sounds: 'employees minus employees-with-departments'.

pitfalls: UNION when UNION ALL was sufficient (paying for a useless sort).
Column count mismatch across branches.
ORDER BY inside a branch instead of at the end.
lessons.try_it: Write: jobs that no employee currently holds

lessons.title: CREATE TABLE Done Right
concepts: Choose types deliberately: NUMBER(p,s) for exact numerics (money: NUMBER(10,2)), VARCHAR2(n) for strings (VARCHAR2, not VARCHAR — Oracle reserves VARCHAR for future semantics), DATE/TIMESTAMP for time.

Constraints inline or out-of-line: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK. Name them (CONSTRAINT emp_pk PRIMARY KEY) — unnamed constraints get system names that haunt migrations.
DEFAULT values (DEFAULT SYSDATE, DEFAULT 'N/A') and identity columns (GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY) remove application burden. Identity is the modern sequence-backed PK — prefer it for new tables.
CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) builds a table from a query — the fastest way to snapshot or restructure data. It copies data, not constraints or indexes: add those after.

example.code:
CREATE TABLE employees (
  employee_id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
    CONSTRAINT emp_pk PRIMARY KEY,
  email VARCHAR2(100) CONSTRAINT emp_email_uq UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  salary NUMBER(10,2) CONSTRAINT emp_sal_ck CHECK (salary > 0),
  department_id NUMBER CONSTRAINT emp_dept_fk REFERENCES departments(department_id)
);
example.walkthrough: Named constraints, typed money, identity PK — the whole discipline in one statement.

pitfalls: VARCHAR instead of VARCHAR2.
Unnamed constraints with SYS_C names.
FLOAT for currency columns.
lessons.try_it: Write CREATE TABLE for a projects table

lessons.title: ALTER TABLE and Schema Evolution
concepts: ALTER TABLE ADD adds columns (with DEFAULT to backfill); MODIFY changes type/length (widening VARCHAR2 is safe, narrowing fails if data overflows); DROP COLUMN removes (SET UNUSED first on huge tables to avoid long locks).
Adding NOT NULL to a populated column fails if NULLs exist — backfill first, then add the constraint. Order matters: UPDATE, then ALTER.
Renames: ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO ...; RENAME COLUMN. Views, procedures, and triggers referencing the old name break — search dependencies (user_dependencies) before renaming.
Online redefinition exists for zero-downtime restructures, but the exam tests the fundamentals: know which ALTER operations lock the table and plan maintenance windows accordingly.

example.walkthrough: Backfill, then constrain — the two-step that the single-step attempt skips.

pitfalls: Adding NOT NULL before backfilling NULLs.
Narrowing a column that holds longer data.
Renaming without checking dependent objects.
lessons.try_it: Add a hire_status column safely to employees

lessons.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE
concepts: INSERT with explicit column lists (never rely on positional order); INSERT ALL inserts one source row into many tables — the exam's multi-table insert answer.
UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE hit every row — the most expensive typo in SQL. Habit: write the WHERE first, or wrap in a transaction and check ROWCOUNT before committing.
MERGE (upsert): WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE / WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT, with optional DELETE clause. One pass over the source — the bulk-load workhorse.
DML and transactions: every DML runs inside a transaction; COMMIT makes it permanent, ROLLBACK undoes. Autocommit in tools commits each statement — know your tool's default before bulk loads.

example.code:
INSERT ALL
  INTO employees (employee_id, first_name) VALUES (emp_id, fname)
  INTO emp_audit (employee_id, action) VALUES (emp_id, 'HIRE')
SELECT 207 AS emp_id, 'Ada' AS fname FROM DUAL;
example.walkthrough: INSERT ALL fans one source row out to many tables — audit and base in one statement.

pitfalls: UPDATE without WHERE.
Positional INSERT depending on column order.
Assuming autocommit is off (or on) without checking.
lessons.try_it: Write a MERGE that also deletes departed employees

lessons.title: Indexes: B-Tree, Bitmap, Function-Based
concepts: B-tree indexes serve high-cardinality equality/range lookups (PKs, IDs, dates). Bitmap indexes serve low-cardinality columns (gender, status) in data warehouses — terrible for heavy OLTP updates.
Composite indexes: column order matters — leading column must appear in the predicate. Index (dept, salary) helps WHERE dept = X AND salary > Y, not WHERE salary > Y alone.
Function-based indexes index expressions: UPPER(email) for case-insensitive search. The query must use the exact expression to match the index.
Index cost: every index slows DML and consumes space. Index foreign keys (avoid locking the parent on child updates) and filter columns; do not index everything 'just in case'.

example.walkthrough: The function-based index only fires when the query's expression matches exactly.

pitfalls: Bitmap index on a heavily-updated OLTP column.
Composite index with the filtered column second and unfiltered first.
Indexing every column — write throughput collapses.
lessons.try_it: Choose indexes for 3 query patterns

lessons.title: Views, Sequences, and Synonyms
concepts: Views encapsulate queries: CREATE VIEW high_earners AS SELECT ... — consumers query the view, the definition stays in one place. Complex views (joins, aggregates) are read-only unless INSTEAD OF triggers intervene.
Materialized views store the result and refresh on demand or commit — the answer for expensive aggregations queried often. Stale data is the tradeoff; schedule refreshes to match tolerance.

Sequences (or identity columns) generate surrogate keys: CREATE SEQUENCE emp_seq START WITH 1000 INCREMENT BY 1. Gaps are normal (cached, rolled-back values vanish) — never use sequences for gapless numbering.
Synonyms alias objects across schemas: app code references EMPLOYEES (synonym) while the table lives in HR schema. Moving the table means repointing the synonym, not rewriting the app.

example.code:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW dept_stats
REFRESH COMPLETE ON DEMAND AS
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) n, AVG(salary) avg_sal
FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
example.walkthrough: The aggregation runs once at refresh; queries hit the stored result — seconds become milliseconds.

pitfalls: Expecting gapless sequence numbers for invoices.
Querying a stale materialized view as if real-time.
Updating through a complex view without INSTEAD OF.
lessons.try_it: Decide view vs materialized view for 3 cases

lessons.title: String Functions
concepts: SUBSTR(s, start, len), INSTR(s, sub) for position, LENGTH, TRIM/LTRIM/RTRIM, UPPER/LOWER/INITCAP. Oracle strings are 1-indexed — SUBSTR('hello', 2, 3) = 'ell'.
Concatenation: || operator (Oracle idiom) or CONCAT (two args only). 'First' || ' ' || 'Last' — NULL || 'x' = 'x' in Oracle (empty-string-is-NULL semantics), unlike most databases.
REGEXP_LIKE/REGEXP_SUBSTR/REGEXP_REPLACE for patterns: email validation, extracting codes. Powerful and slow — use plain functions when they suffice.
LPAD/RPAD for formatting, REPLACE/TRANSLATE for character swaps. TRANSLATE does per-character mapping in one pass — faster than nested REPLACEs.

example.walkthrough: INSTR finds the @; SUBSTR takes everything before it — parsing without regex.

pitfalls: 0-indexed SUBSTR assumptions from other languages.
CONCAT with three arguments.
Regex where SUBSTR/INSTR would do.
lessons.try_it: Extract area codes from a phone column

lessons.title: Number and Date Functions
concepts: ROUND(n, d), TRUNC(n, d) (truncate, not round), MOD, CEIL/FLOOR, ABS. TRUNC(salary, -3) rounds down to thousands — the banding trick without CASE.
Date arithmetic: SYSDATE, ADD_MONTHS(d, n), MONTHS_BETWEEN, NEXT_DAY, LAST_DAY, TRUNC(d, 'MM') for month-start. Dates subtract to give days: hire_date - SYSDATE.
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d), TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYY-MM-DD') for formatting, TO_DATE(s, 'format') for parsing. Format-model mismatches are the top date bug — 'DD-MON-RR' vs the actual string.
INTERVAL arithmetic: SYSTIMESTAMP + INTERVAL '2' HOUR. Timestamps with time zones (TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE) for global apps — store in UTC, display in local.

example.code:
SELECT first_name,
       TRUNC(MONTHS_BETWEEN(SYSDATE, hire_date)/12) AS years,
       ADD_MONTHS(hire_date, 12) AS first_anniversary
FROM employees;
example.walkthrough: MONTHS_BETWEEN/12 truncated = whole years of service — the tenure calculation.

pitfalls: ROUND when TRUNC was needed (banding).
Comparing DATE to a string without TO_DATE.
Assuming date subtraction gives months.
lessons.try_it: Compute tenure bands with TRUNC

lessons.title: NULL Handling: NVL, COALESCE, NULLIF
concepts: NVL(a, b): if a is NULL return b (Oracle-specific, two args). COALESCE(a, b, c, ...): first non-NULL (standard, short-circuits). NVL2(a, b, c): b if a not null else c.
NULLIF(a, b): NULL if a = b — the divide-by-zero guard: salary / NULLIF(months, 0). LNNVL for complex 'not true including NULL' predicates in exotic cases.
Aggregates ignore NULLs (except COUNT(*)); arithmetic with NULL yields NULL. Wrap nullable inputs: SUM(NVL(bonus, 0)) not SUM(bonus) when missing means zero.
Empty string IS NULL in Oracle: '' = NULL. WHERE col = '' never matches — a standing Oracle gotcha for developers from other databases.

example.walkthrough: NVL turns 'unknown commission' into 'zero commission' — a business decision encoded in one function.

pitfalls: SUM(bonus) treating missing as zero without NVL.
WHERE col = '' expecting matches.
= NULL comparisons (still).
lessons.try_it: Fix a total-comp query for NULL commissions

lessons.title: Analytic Function Basics
concepts: Analytic functions compute across rows without collapsing them: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), SUM() OVER (...). The OVER clause defines the window — PARTITION BY groups, ORDER BY sequences.
ROW_NUMBER gives unique 1..n (ties broken arbitrarily); RANK gives 1,1,3 (gaps); DENSE_RANK gives 1,1,2. 'Top 3 with ties' = RANK/DENSE_RANK, not ROW_NUMBER.
Running totals: SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY hire_date) — cumulative per department in hire order. The ORDER BY inside OVER defines the accumulation sequence.
LAG/LEAD peek at previous/next rows: LAG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY effective_date) — prior value per employee, the trend-analysis primitive.

example.code:
SELECT first_name, salary,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS pay_rank,
  SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) AS dept_total
FROM employees;
example.walkthrough: Same query, two windows: global rank and departmental total — analytics without GROUP BY collapse.

pitfalls: ROW_NUMBER for 'top 3 including ties'.
Missing PARTITION BY — window spans the whole table.
ORDER BY inside OVER forgotten on running totals.
lessons.try_it: Rank earners and show dept running totals

lessons.title: Conversion and Formatting Functions
concepts: TO_CHAR/TO_NUMBER/TO_DATE with explicit format models — never rely on NLS defaults. TO_CHAR(1234.5, '9999.99'), TO_DATE('2026-10-10', 'YYYY-MM-DD').
CAST(x AS type) is the standard syntax; Oracle also has the legacy conversions. CAST is portable; TO_* is Oracle-idiomatic — know both, the exam uses both.
Formatting numbers: TO_CHAR(salary, '$999,999.99') for reports. Formatting is presentation — do it in SELECT for display, never store formatted strings.
Implicit conversion is the enemy: comparing a VARCHAR2 column to a number converts every row (killing indexes) or raises ORA-01722 on bad data. Convert explicitly, once, on the literal side.

example.walkthrough: Convert the literal, not the column — the index survives and bad input fails fast.

pitfalls: Relying on NLS date formats in TO_DATE.
Comparing number columns to string literals.
Storing formatted currency strings.
lessons.try_it: Format a salary report with TO_CHAR

lessons.title: Block Structure and Variables
concepts: Anonymous block anatomy: DECLARE (variables), BEGIN (logic), EXCEPTION (handlers), END. Only BEGIN..END is mandatory — DECLARE and EXCEPTION appear as needed.
Variables: name TYPE [NOT NULL] [:= default]; %TYPE anchors to a column (v_sal employees.salary%TYPE) — the variable tracks schema changes automatically. %ROWTYPE anchors a whole row.
Scope: variables declared in an inner block shadow outer ones; inner blocks see outer variables. Keep blocks small — shadowing bugs are silent.
DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE for debugging; SET SERVEROUTPUT ON to see it. It is a debug tool, not an application interface — never build logic on its output.

example.walkthrough: %TYPE means the variable survives a column-type change — hardcoded NUMBER(10,2) does not.

pitfalls: SELECT without INTO in PL/SQL — 'exact fetch returns no rows' confusion.
Hardcoded types instead of %TYPE.
Variable shadowing across nested blocks.
lessons.try_it: Write a block printing the employee count

lessons.title: Control Flow: IF, CASE, Loops
concepts: IF/ELSIF/ELSE for branching; searched CASE for multi-way. ELSIF is one word — 'ELSE IF' is a syntax error, an exam favorite.
Loops: LOOP..EXIT WHEN (manual), WHILE (condition first), FOR i IN 1..10 (auto-counter). FOR rec IN (SELECT ...) loops query rows directly — the cursor-FOR-loop idiom.
Cursor FOR loop: FOR r IN (SELECT * FROM employees) LOOP ... END LOOP — opens, fetches, closes automatically. The cleanest row-by-row pattern; prefer set SQL when possible.
EXIT/CONTINUE with labels for nested loops. Row-by-row is the last resort — 'slow by slow' processing; always ask whether one SQL statement could replace the loop.

example.walkthrough: Cursor FOR loop: no DECLARE, no OPEN/FETCH/CLOSE — the loop manages the cursor.

pitfalls: ELSE IF instead of ELSIF.
Row-by-row where one UPDATE would do.
EXIT WHEN forgotten — infinite LOOP.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite a loop as a single UPDATE

lessons.title: Cursors: Explicit and Attributes
concepts: Explicit cursor: DECLARE CURSOR c IS SELECT ...; OPEN; FETCH INTO; EXIT WHEN c%NOTFOUND; CLOSE. Needed when you must control fetching manually — rare; cursor FOR loops cover most cases.
Cursor attributes: %FOUND, %NOTFOUND, %ROWCOUNT, %ISOPEN. SQL%ROWCOUNT after DML tells you how many rows were hit — check it before committing bulk operations.
Parameterized cursors: CURSOR c(p_dept NUMBER) IS SELECT ... WHERE department_id = p_dept — reusable logic with different inputs, the cursor as a function.
SELECT ... INTO must return exactly one row: NO_DATA_FOUND (zero) and TOO_MANY_ROWS (many) are exceptions to handle, not bugs to fear — handle them in EXCEPTION.

example.walkthrough: Parameterized cursor + FOR loop: reusable query, automatic lifecycle — the best of both.

pitfalls: Manual OPEN/FETCH/CLOSE when a FOR loop would do.
Ignoring SQL%ROWCOUNT before COMMIT on bulk DML.
Unhandled NO_DATA_FOUND crashing the block.
lessons.try_it: Handle NO_DATA_FOUND gracefully in a block

lessons.title: Exception Handling
concepts: EXCEPTION block with WHEN handlers: WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN ..., WHEN OTHERS THEN ... (last, and re-raise or log — swallowing OTHERS hides bugs). Named exceptions via PRAGMA EXCEPTION_INIT for specific ORA- codes.
RAISE re-throws the current exception; RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20001, 'message') raises custom errors in the -20000..-20999 range — the API's way of saying 'business rule violated'.
Unhandled exceptions propagate to the caller and roll back to the last COMMIT — understand the blast radius: a failed procedure rolls back its uncommitted work, not the caller's earlier commits.
Log errors to a table (autonomous transaction so the log survives the rollback), then re-raise. Debugging without an error log is archaeology.

example.walkthrough: Log, then RAISE — the caller still sees the failure, and you keep the evidence.

pitfalls: WHEN OTHERS without RAISE — silent failure.
Custom errors outside -20000..-20999.
Error logging rolled back with the transaction.
lessons.try_it: Add proper handlers to yesterday's block

lessons.title: Records, Collections, Bulk Ops
concepts: Records group fields: rec employees%ROWTYPE holds a whole row. Collections: associative arrays (index-by tables), nested tables, varrays — in-memory lists for batch processing.
BULK COLLECT fetches many rows at once: SELECT ... BULK COLLECT INTO coll — one context switch instead of thousands. Pair with FORALL for bulk DML.
FORALL i IN 1..coll.COUNT INSERT ... — sends the whole batch in one round trip. FORALL is not a loop; it is a bulk bind. The performance difference is orders of magnitude.
SAVE EXCEPTIONS collects per-row errors: FORALL ... SAVE EXCEPTIONS, then inspect SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS — bulk loads that tolerate bad rows without aborting.

example.walkthrough: BULK COLLECT + FORALL: fetch once, update in bulk — the fast path for batch PL/SQL.

pitfalls: Row-by-row FETCH in a LOOP for 100k rows.
FORALL written as a regular FOR loop.
BULK COLLECT without LIMIT on huge tables — memory blowout.
lessons.try_it: Convert a slow loop to BULK COLLECT + FORALL

lessons.title: Procedures and Functions
concepts: CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE name(params) — params are IN (default), OUT, or IN OUT. Procedures do work; functions return values. Call procedures with EXEC or in a block; functions in SQL or assignments.
Parameter modes: IN is read-only input; OUT returns values; IN OUT both. Default values (p_x NUMBER := 0) make params optional — call with named notation (p_x => 5) for clarity.

Functions in SQL must be well-behaved: no DML on the calling statement's table (mutating-table error), deterministic where possible. A function that queries other tables per row is a performance trap.
AUTHID CURRENT_USER vs DEFINER: definer's rights (default) run with the owner's privileges; invoker's rights run with the caller's. Choose deliberately — privilege bugs hide here.

example.walkthrough: The business rule lives in the procedure — every caller is bound by it, no exceptions.

pitfalls: OUT param read before assignment.
Function with DML called from a SELECT.
Positional args on a 6-param procedure — use named notation.
lessons.try_it: Write a transfer_employee procedure

lessons.title: Package Spec and Body
concepts: Packages bundle related procedures/functions: the spec declares the public API (visible), the body implements it plus private helpers (hidden). Change the body without invalidating callers — the spec is the contract.
Package state: variables declared in the body persist for the session — useful for caching, dangerous for correctness (stale state across calls). Prefer stateless unless caching is the point.
Initialization block: runs once per session on first use — sets up state, validates environment. Overloading: same procedure name, different signatures — one name, many arities.
Forward declarations in the body let private procedures call each other regardless of order. Keep the spec minimal: everything public is a maintenance commitment.

example.walkthrough: Three public operations, zero exposed internals — the spec is all a consumer needs.

pitfalls: All logic in the spec — no encapsulation.
Session-persistent state assumed fresh per call.
Public procedures that should have been private.
lessons.try_it: Design a spec for the capstone mart API

lessons.title: DML Triggers: Timing and Granularity
concepts: Trigger timing: BEFORE (validate/transform before the write), AFTER (audit/react after). Granularity: FOR EACH ROW (per-row, sees :OLD/:NEW) vs statement-level (once per statement, no row values).
Audit pattern: AFTER UPDATE OF salary ON employees FOR EACH ROW -> insert :OLD/:NEW into audit table. Statement-level triggers cannot see row values — choose row-level for auditing.
BEFORE triggers can modify :NEW values (normalize input, set defaults, validate and RAISE). AFTER triggers cannot change the row — the write already happened.
Mutating-table error: a row trigger querying its own table. Restructure: statement trigger, compound trigger, or (best) move the logic out of the trigger into the API procedure.

example.walkthrough: BEFORE row trigger: normalize and validate before the row exists — invalid data never lands.

pitfalls: AFTER trigger trying to modify :NEW.
Row trigger SELECTing from its own table.
Business logic duplicated in triggers and app code.
lessons.try_it: Write an audit trigger for job changes

lessons.title: Compound and System Triggers
concepts: Compound triggers have timing sections (BEFORE STATEMENT, BEFORE EACH ROW, AFTER EACH ROW, AFTER STATEMENT) sharing state — the clean fix for mutating-table problems: collect row IDs per-row, process once at statement level.
INSTEAD OF triggers on views make complex views updatable: the trigger translates the view DML into base-table DML. The view stays the interface; the trigger does the mapping.
System triggers: ON LOGON/LOGOFF, DDL triggers (BEFORE CREATE ...), ON SHUTDOWN. DDL triggers audit schema changes — 'who dropped that table?' answered from the log.
Trigger discipline: triggers are invisible logic — document every trigger's purpose, keep them small, and prefer API procedures for business rules. A database full of triggers is undebuggable.

example.walkthrough: Row section collects, statement section acts — the mutating-table workaround in one object.

pitfalls: Business rules hidden in 20 triggers instead of the API.
Undocumented triggers — invisible logic.
DDL changes with no audit trigger to record them.
lessons.try_it: List every trigger's purpose in one table

lessons.title: Dependencies and Invalidation
concepts: Objects depend on each other: procedures on tables, views on tables, triggers on tables. user_dependencies maps the graph — query it before ALTERing anything.

DDL on a base object invalidates dependents (status = INVALID); Oracle recompiles automatically on next use, but runtime recompilation means the first caller pays — and compilation can fail if the change broke the contract.
Edition-based redefinition and careful deployment order (tables -> views -> packages -> triggers) minimize invalid windows. Deploy in dependency order, verify status after.
DBMS_UTILITY.COMPILE_SCHEMA recompiles a schema's invalid objects after a change. Check user_objects for INVALID as a deploy step — red in the deploy log, not in production at 2 AM.

example.walkthrough: Invalid-object check is a deploy gate: zero INVALID before sign-off.

pitfalls: Deploying tables after the packages that use them.
Never checking for INVALID objects post-deploy.
Renaming a column without finding dependents first.
lessons.try_it: Map dependencies before an ALTER

lessons.title: Window Functions Deep Dive
concepts: Window functions keep row detail while computing group values: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK for ranking; SUM/AVG with OVER for running totals; the frame clause (ROWS BETWEEN) controls exactly which rows participate.
Ranking done right: ROW_NUMBER for dedup and pagination, RANK/DENSE_RANK for 'top N with ties'. Picking the wrong one silently drops tied rows — a classic exam trap.

Frames: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (running total), ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING (moving average). The default frame (RANGE ... CURRENT ROW) misbehaves with duplicate ORDER BY values.
Named windows: WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY sal) lets multiple functions share one definition — cleaner and the optimizer computes it once.

example.code:
SELECT employee_id, salary,
  AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id
    ORDER BY hire_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma3
FROM employees;
example.walkthrough: PARTITION BY department_id resets the window per department; the 3-row frame gives a moving average.

pitfalls: RANGE default frame with duplicate sort keys — wrong moving averages.
ROW_NUMBER when ties must be kept.
Repeating the window definition instead of naming it.
lessons.try_it: Write a 3-month moving average of hires per dept

lessons.title: Subquery Factoring and CTE Patterns
concepts: Chained CTEs build queries as pipelines: raw -> cleaned -> aggregated -> ranked. Each CTE has one job; the final SELECT is a simple assembly. Debugging means testing one CTE at a time.
CTEs vs inline views: identical performance (Oracle may materialize either), but CTEs are reusable within the query — reference the same CTE three times without rewriting it.
Recursive CTEs with CONNECT BY for hierarchies and graphs: org charts, BOM explosions, path finding. LEVEL, CONNECT_BY_ROOT, SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH are the hierarchy toolkit.
The 'filter early' rule: put WHERE inside the CTE, not after — filtering 10M rows to 1K before the join beats joining then filtering. Predicate placement is the cheapest optimization.

example.walkthrough: Two thoughts, two CTEs: aggregate, then rank. Each is testable alone.

pitfalls: Filtering after the CTE instead of inside it.
One mega-CTE doing five jobs.
Recursive query without NOCYCLE on cyclic data.
lessons.try_it: Refactor a 60-line query into chained CTEs

lessons.title: PIVOT, UNPIVOT, and Crosstabs
concepts: PIVOT rotates rows into columns: sales rows per quarter become one row per product with Q1..Q4 columns. The IN list defines the output columns — dynamic pivots need dynamic SQL or XML variants.
UNPIVOT does the reverse: wide tables (jan, feb, mar columns) become tall (month, value) rows — the normalization step before analysis. Wide-to-tall is the common direction in reporting.
Conditional aggregation (SUM(CASE WHEN quarter='Q1' THEN amt END)) is the portable pivot — works everywhere, explicit, and often clearer than PIVOT syntax for a few columns.
XML PIVOT handles unknown-at-write-time values, returning XML you parse later. Rare in exams, but the answer when 'the columns aren't known until runtime'.

example.code:
SELECT * FROM (SELECT department_id, job_id, salary FROM employees)
PIVOT (AVG(salary) FOR job_id IN ('SA_MAN' AS sales_mgr, 'IT_PROG' AS programmer));
example.walkthrough: The FOR ... IN list becomes the columns; each cell is the aggregate for that (dept, job) pair.

pitfalls: PIVOT without knowing the IN values must be static.
Expecting PIVOT to auto-discover columns.
Pivoting before filtering — aggregate the filtered set.
lessons.try_it: Pivot headcount by dept and job

lessons.title: Hierarchical Queries and CONNECT BY
concepts: START WITH defines roots, CONNECT BY PRIOR links parent to child: CONNECT BY PRIOR employee_id = manager_id walks down the org chart. PRIOR marks the parent-side column.
LEVEL pseudocolumn = depth from root (1-based); LPAD(' ', 2*(LEVEL-1)) || name indents the tree visually. CONNECT_BY_ROOT(col) carries the root's value down every row — 'which CEO's org is this in'.
SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(name, ' -> ') builds the full path string per row — the breadcrumb. NOCYCLE stops infinite loops on bad data; CONNECT_BY_ISCYCLE flags the offending rows.
ORDER SIBLINGS BY sorts within each level while preserving the tree shape — regular ORDER BY flattens the hierarchy. The exam loves this distinction.

example.code:
SELECT LEVEL, LPAD(' ', 2*(LEVEL-1)) || last_name AS org,
       CONNECT_BY_ROOT last_name AS ceo
FROM employees
START WITH manager_id IS NULL
CONNECT BY NOCYCLE PRIOR employee_id = manager_id
ORDER SIBLINGS BY last_name;
example.walkthrough: NOCYCLE guards the walk; ORDER SIBLINGS BY keeps the tree readable; the root rides along via CONNECT_BY_ROOT.

pitfalls: ORDER BY instead of ORDER SIBLINGS BY — flat list.
PRIOR on the wrong side — walks up instead of down.
No NOCYCLE on production hierarchies.
lessons.try_it: Draw your schema's hierarchy with LEVEL

lessons.title: Analytic Patterns: Top-N per Group, Gaps, Dedup
concepts: Top-N per group: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC), then filter rn <= N in an outer query — the canonical pattern. Analytic functions can't appear in WHERE, hence the subquery wrap.
Gaps and islands: LAG/LEAD compare consecutive rows to find breaks (session boundaries, missing sequences). row_number - value groups consecutive integers into islands — the famous trick.
Dedup: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dup_key ORDER BY keep_priority) then DELETE rn > 1 — keeps the best copy of each duplicate set. Far safer than DISTINCT-based deletes.
Year-over-year: LAG(sales, 12) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month) — prior-year same month, the growth calculation in one expression.

example.walkthrough: Partition, rank, wrap, filter — the four beats of every top-N-per-group query.

pitfalls: Analytic function directly in WHERE — not allowed.
RANK when dedup needs exactly one survivor.
LAG without PARTITION — prior row leaks across groups.
lessons.try_it: Find the top 3 products per category

lessons.title: Regular Expressions in SQL
concepts: REGEXP_LIKE for pattern matching in WHERE, REGEXP_SUBSTR to extract, REGEXP_REPLACE to transform, REGEXP_INSTR for positions, REGEXP_COUNT to count occurrences — the full regex toolkit in SQL.
Validation patterns: email '^[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$', phone digits '^[0-9]{10}$'. Validate at the CHECK-constraint or query level, not just the app.
Extraction: REGEXP_SUBSTR(email, '[^@]+') grabs the local part; capture groups with the subexpr parameter pull the nth group — parse structured strings without app code.
Cost: regex is 10-100x slower than LIKE/SUBSTR — never regex a million-row scan when a plain function works. Use regex for complexity, plain functions for speed.

example.walkthrough: Negated validation query: finds exactly the rows that violate the format — the data-quality audit.

pitfalls: Regex on huge scans where LIKE would do.
No anchor ^$ — partial matches accepted as valid.
Escaping the dot in the domain part forgotten.
lessons.try_it: Find malformed phone numbers with REGEXP_LIKE

lessons.title: Reading Execution Plans
concepts: EXPLAIN PLAN FOR <query> then SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY) — the plan shows the optimizer's chosen path: access methods, join order, join methods, estimated rows and cost.
Read inside-out, top-down: the most indented operation runs first; siblings run top-to-bottom. TABLE ACCESS FULL vs INDEX RANGE SCAN vs INDEX UNIQUE SCAN tells you how each table is reached.
Cardinality estimates vs reality: E-Rows (estimated) vs A-Rows (actual, with GATHER_PLAN_STATISTICS). A 100x gap means stale stats or bad predicates — the root of most 'slow query' mysteries.
The plan is a prediction, not a measurement: cost is the optimizer's guess. Confirm with actual runtime stats before tuning — tuning the wrong operation wastes days.

example.walkthrough: Even this trivial plan teaches the reading order: indent depth = execution order.

pitfalls: Tuning without looking at the plan.
Trusting cost as wall-clock time.
Ignoring the E-Rows/A-Rows gap.
lessons.try_it: Explain your three slowest queries

lessons.title: Optimizer Statistics
concepts: The optimizer's decisions come from statistics: DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS collects row counts, distinct values, histograms. Stale stats = wrong plans = slow queries after data changes.
Histograms matter for skewed columns: without one, the optimizer assumes uniform distribution and misestimates selective predicates badly. STATUS='ACTIVE' with 99% 'Y' needs a histogram.
Auto stats gathering runs nightly by default — know it exists, and know when to gather manually after bulk loads (a 10M-row load at noon waits for midnight stats otherwise).
Locking stats (LOCK_TABLE_STATS) freezes plans for volatile tables; pending stats let you test new stats before publishing. Plan stability is a feature, not an accident.

example.walkthrough: AUTO sample size and AUTO histograms — the modern default that gets it right.

pitfalls: Bulk load then wondering why plans went bad.
Deleting stats instead of gathering.
No histograms on skewed filter columns.
lessons.try_it: Check last_analyzed on your key tables

lessons.title: Join Methods and Indexes
concepts: Three join methods: NESTED LOOPS (small outer, indexed inner — OLTP), HASH JOIN (large sets, no useful index — warehouse), SORT MERGE (pre-sorted inputs, rare). The optimizer picks by size estimates — wrong estimates pick wrong methods.
Index design follows predicates: equality columns first, then range; covering indexes (all selected columns in the index) avoid table access entirely — INDEX ONLY scans on wide queries.
The clustering factor measures how ordered the table is vs the index — high factor means an index range scan jumps all over the disk, and the optimizer correctly prefers a full scan.
Invisible indexes test safely: make an index INVISIBLE, watch performance, drop or keep — no plan changes until you flip it visible. Zero-risk index experiments.

example.walkthrough: All selected and filtered columns are in the index — the table access vanishes from the plan.

pitfalls: Index on every column — DML crawls.
Range column first in a composite index.
Forgetting the clustering factor on range scans.
lessons.try_it: Design covering indexes for 3 reports

lessons.title: Hints and Plan Control
concepts: Hints override the optimizer: /*+ INDEX(e emp_ix) */, /*+ FULL(e) */, /*+ LEADING(d e) */ (join order), /*+ USE_HASH(e d) */ (join method), /*+ PARALLEL(4) */. Hints are directives with a plus sign — misspelled hints are silently ignored comments.
Hint discipline: hints fix the symptom (this query's plan), statistics fix the cause. A hinted query rots as data changes — document why each hint exists and revisit it.
SQL Plan Baselines capture known-good plans and only allow better ones — the production-grade answer to plan flips after upgrades. Baselines beat hints for stability.
SQL Profiles add optimizer corrections without changing the query text — useful for packaged apps you cannot modify. Three layers: fix stats, baseline the plan, hint as last resort.

example.code:
SELECT /*+ LEADING(d) USE_HASH(e) */ e.first_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
example.walkthrough: LEADING sets the join order, USE_HASH the method — explicit control when the optimizer guesses wrong.

pitfalls: Hinting before checking statistics.
Undocumented hints rotting for years.
Misspelled hint silently ignored.
lessons.try_it: Find and justify every hint in your codebase

lessons.title: Bulk Operations and Array Processing
concepts: Context switches between SQL and PL/SQL engines are the hidden tax: row-by-row loops pay it per row. BULK COLLECT fetches in arrays; FORALL binds DML in arrays — 10-100x faster.
BULK COLLECT with LIMIT n processes in chunks — full collect on 10M rows exhausts PGA. LIMIT 1000 in a loop is the production pattern.
FORALL ... SAVE EXCEPTIONS continues past bad rows, logging them in SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS — bulk loads that tolerate dirty data without aborting the batch.
APPEND hint / direct-path inserts bypass the buffer cache for bulk loads: INSERT /*+ APPEND */ — fast, but locks exclusively and needs NOLOGGING awareness for recoverability.

example.walkthrough: Chunked bulk collect + forall with save exceptions — the production bulk-load loop.

pitfalls: Unlimited BULK COLLECT on huge tables.
Row-by-row INSERT in a 1M-row loop.
Direct-path insert without understanding NOLOGGING.
lessons.try_it: Convert a slow loader to bulk

lessons.title: Common Anti-Patterns
concepts: SELECT * in production code: fetches unneeded LOBs, breaks covering indexes, and couples the app to column order. List columns explicitly — always.
Functions on indexed columns in WHERE (WHERE UPPER(email) = ...) defeat the index — use function-based indexes or rewrite. Implicit conversions do the same damage silently.
N+1 queries: one query for the list, then one per row for details — 1001 round trips. Fix with a join or bulk fetch. ORMs generate these; the fix is at the query design level.
Correlated subqueries in SELECT for aggregates: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.cust = c.id) per row — rewrite as a GROUP BY join. One pass beats N probes.

example.code:
-- N+1 anti-pattern: 1 + N round trips
-- fix: single join
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
example.walkthrough: The join computes all counts in one pass — the N+1 collapses to 1 query.

pitfalls: SELECT * 'for convenience'.
Correlated aggregate subqueries in SELECT.
LIKE '%x%' on an indexed column expecting index use.
lessons.try_it: Find N+1 queries in your app's logs

lessons.title: ACID and Transaction Boundaries
concepts: ACID: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (concurrent txns don't corrupt each other), Durability (committed = permanent). Every COMMIT is a durability promise.
Transaction boundaries are yours to choose: one business operation = one transaction. COMMIT too often breaks atomicity (half a transfer commits); too rarely holds locks and bloats undo.
Implicit vs explicit: DDL auto-commits before and after; DML waits for your COMMIT. A CREATE INDEX in the middle of a load commits the load — plan DDL outside transactions.
Autonomous transactions (PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION) commit independently — the error-logging pattern: log the failure even though the main transaction rolls back.

example.walkthrough: Both updates commit together or not at all — atomicity is the transfer's correctness.

pitfalls: DDL inside a transaction expecting rollback.
COMMIT after every statement in a multi-step op.
Autonomous txn for business data — commits you can't roll back.
lessons.try_it: Define transaction boundaries for 3 operations

lessons.title: Isolation Levels and Read Consistency
concepts: Oracle's default READ COMMITTED: each statement sees committed data as of statement start — multiversion read consistency via undo. Readers never block writers, writers never block readers.

SERIALIZABLE: the transaction sees data as of transaction start — repeatable reads, but concurrent writes to the same rows raise ORA-08177 (can't serialize). Use for critical computations, retry on conflict.
READ ONLY transactions for reporting: consistent snapshot, no locks, guaranteed repeatable — the long-report answer. SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY at the start.
Lost updates: two sessions read 100, both write 110 — one update lost. Prevent with SELECT FOR UPDATE (pessimistic lock) or optimistic version columns.

example.code:
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
-- row locked; other sessions wait (or skip with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
example.walkthrough: FOR UPDATE takes the row lock before the change — the lost-update fix for queue-style workloads.

pitfalls: Assuming READ COMMITTED gives repeatable reads.
No locking on read-modify-write cycles.
SERIALIZABLE without a retry loop.
lessons.try_it: Demonstrate a lost update, then fix it

lessons.title: Locking: Rows, Tables, Deadlocks
concepts: Row locks (TX) are held until COMMIT/ROLLBACK — the normal case. Table locks (TM) come from unindexed foreign keys: child DML locks the parent table. Index your FKs.

Deadlock: session A locks row 1 waits for row 2; session B holds 2 waits for 1 — Oracle detects and kills one with ORA-00060. Fix by consistent lock ordering (always parent-then-child, or ORDER BY id).
Lock waits: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE WAIT 5 / NOWAIT / SKIP LOCKED — control the behavior. SKIP LOCKED is the work-queue primitive: many workers, no waiting, no double-processing.
DDL locks: DDL needs exclusive access — a long transaction blocks your ALTER. Check v$locked_object / DBA_BLOCKERS before blaming the DDL.

example.walkthrough: SKIP LOCKED turns the table into a concurrent queue — workers never block each other.

pitfalls: Unindexed FK causing TM lock storms.
Inconsistent lock order across code paths.
FOR UPDATE without a timeout on interactive sessions.
lessons.try_it: Build a SKIP LOCKED work queue

lessons.title: Undo, Redo, and Flashback
concepts: Undo stores before-images for read consistency and rollback; redo logs every change for recovery. A transaction generates both — size your undo tablespace for the longest concurrent transaction.
ORA-01555 snapshot too old: the query ran longer than undo retention — the before-image aged out. Fix: bigger undo, shorter queries, or flashback-friendly retention (RETENTION GUARANTEE).
Flashback Query: SELECT ... AS OF TIMESTAMP (SYSTIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '1' HOUR) — time travel for 'what did this look like before the bad update'. The oops-recovery tool.
Flashback Table / Drop (recycle bin): FLASHBACK TABLE t TO BEFORE DROP recovers dropped tables — until purged. The safety net under every DROP.

example.code:
-- what did salaries look like an hour ago?
SELECT employee_id, salary FROM employees
AS OF TIMESTAMP (SYSTIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '1' HOUR)
WHERE department_id = 50;
example.walkthrough: AS OF TIMESTAMP reads the undo-kept past — forensics without a restore.

pitfalls: ORA-01555 on long reports — fix undo, not the query.
PURGE recyclebin before verifying the drop was wrong.
Assuming flashback survives DDL — it doesn't always.

lessons.title: Savepoints and Partial Rollback
concepts: SAVEPOINT s1 marks a point; ROLLBACK TO s1 undoes only the work after it — partial rollback within a transaction. The transaction continues; earlier work is intact.
Use savepoints for 'try this step, fall back if it fails': bulk load with per-batch savepoints — a bad batch rolls back to its savepoint, good batches stay.
Savepoints don't release locks — rolled-back-to-savepoint rows stay locked until COMMIT. Partial rollback is about data, not concurrency.
Nested procedures and savepoints: a procedure can set savepoints for its own steps without affecting the caller's earlier work — composable transactions.

example.walkthrough: ROLLBACK TO rewinds to the savepoint — surgical undo inside a larger transaction.

pitfalls: ROLLBACK TO expecting locks to release.
No savepoints in multi-step loads — one bad row kills all.
Savepoint names colliding across nested calls.
lessons.try_it: Add savepoints to a 3-step load

lessons.title: Concurrency Design Patterns
concepts: Optimistic locking: version column, UPDATE ... WHERE id = X AND version = v — zero locks held, conflicts detected at write. The web-app default for low-contention data.
Pessimistic locking: SELECT FOR UPDATE for high-contention, must-not-conflict operations (seat booking, inventory decrement). Holds the lock — keep the transaction short.
Queue tables with SKIP LOCKED for work distribution; partition by hash for parallel workers without contention; sequence caching to avoid SQ enqueue waits on hot sequences.
Design rule: keep transactions short, touch rows in consistent order, lock only what you change, and never hold a transaction open across user think-time.

example.code:
-- optimistic update: version guards the write
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1, version = version + 1
WHERE id = 42 AND version = 7;
-- SQL%ROWCOUNT = 0 means someone else got there first: retry
example.walkthrough: The version check makes the update conditional — conflicts surface as zero rows, not corruption.

pitfalls: Pessimistic locks held across user think-time.
Hot sequence without CACHE on high-insert tables.
No retry logic on optimistic conflicts.

lessons.title: Instance vs Database
concepts: The instance is memory + processes (SGA + background processes); the database is files on disk (datafiles, control files, redo logs). The instance is the running engine; the database is the stored data — the exam tests this split constantly.
SGA components: buffer cache (data blocks), shared pool (parsed SQL + data dictionary), redo log buffer, large pool. PGA is per-server-process memory (sorts, hashes) — SGA is shared, PGA is private.
Background processes: PMON (cleanup), SMON (recovery), DBWn (writes dirty buffers), LGWR (writes redo), CKPT (checkpoints), ARCn (archives redo). Know each one's one-line job.

Startup stages: NOMOUNT (instance only) -> MOUNT (control file) -> OPEN (datafiles). SHUTDOWN modes: NORMAL/TRANSACTIONAL/IMMEDIATE/ABORT — IMMEDIATE is the production default, ABORT needs instance recovery.

example.walkthrough: v$ views expose the running instance; the open_mode confirms the database state.

pitfalls: Calling the datafiles 'the instance'.
SHUTDOWN ABORT as a routine method.
Confusing PGA (private) with SGA (shared).
lessons.try_it: Map each background process to its one-line job

lessons.title: Tablespaces, Datafiles, Segments
concepts: Tablespaces are logical storage containers; datafiles are the physical files. Tables live in tablespaces via segments (table segment, index segment) made of extents made of blocks.
SYSTEM/SYSAUX hold the data dictionary — never put user data there. UNDO tablespace holds undo; TEMP holds sort spill. A full SYSTEM tablespace is an outage.

Locally managed tablespaces with AUTOALLOCATE are the modern default — the database manages extents, not you. Dictionary-managed is legacy; the exam may still mention it to test you know it's obsolete.
Bigfile vs smallfile: bigfile tablespaces have one large datafile (simpler, for huge DBs); smallfile allows many. Default is smallfile — know both exist and when bigfile wins.

example.code:
SELECT tablespace_name, file_name, bytes/1024/1024 AS mb
FROM dba_data_files ORDER BY tablespace_name;
example.walkthrough: dba_data_files maps every logical tablespace to its physical files and sizes.

pitfalls: User tables in SYSTEM/SYSAUX.
Ignoring TEMP/UNDO sizing on load-heavy DBs.
Dictionary-managed tablespaces on new builds.
lessons.try_it: List your tablespaces and their datafiles

lessons.title: Redo, Undo, and Recovery
concepts: Redo logs record every change (for recovery); undo records before-images (for rollback + read consistency). Redo is write-ahead: LGWR writes redo before DBWn writes data — crash recovery replays redo.

ARCHIVELOG mode copies filled redo logs to archive destinations — required for point-in-time recovery and hot backups. NOARCHIVELOG loses everything since the last cold backup. Production = ARCHIVELOG, always.
Checkpoints (CKPT) mark how far recovery must replay; fast-start fault recovery targets bound it. SCNs (system change numbers) order every change — the database's logical clock.
Media recovery: restore datafiles from backup, RECOVER DATABASE applies archived redo — the DBA's core drill. Instance recovery is automatic on startup after a crash (SMON rolls forward/back).

example.walkthrough: Two commands confirm the recovery posture — the first thing to check on any new database.

pitfalls: NOARCHIVELOG on a production database.
Confusing redo (recovery) with undo (rollback).
No tested restore — backups nobody restored.
lessons.try_it: Verify ARCHIVELOG mode on your instance

lessons.title: Data Dictionary and Dynamic Views
concepts: The data dictionary is the read-only metadata: DBA_* (all objects), ALL_* (objects you can access), USER_* (objects you own). DBA_TABLES vs ALL_TABLES vs USER_TABLES — scope shrinks left to right.
V$ dynamic performance views show the running instance: V$SESSION (who's connected), V$SQL (what's executing), V$SYSTEM_EVENT (what it's waiting on). GV$ variants span RAC instances.
CDB/PDB dictionary: CDB_* views see across containers in multitenant. Know whether you're in the root or a PDB — queries behave differently per container.
Dictionary queries are your X-ray: 'which indexes exist on this table' (DBA_INDEXES), 'who's blocking whom' (V$LOCK + V$SESSION), 'what ran long' (V$SQL ordered by elapsed).

example.code:
-- who's blocking whom right now
SELECT s1.username blocker, s2.username waiter
FROM v$lock l1 JOIN v$lock l2 ON l1.id1 = l2.id1
JOIN v$session s1 ON l1.sid = s1.sid
JOIN v$session s2 ON l2.sid = s2.sid
WHERE l1.block = 1 AND l2.request > 0;
example.walkthrough: V$LOCK joined to V$SESSION twice — blockers and waiters in one query.

pitfalls: USER_* when the object is in another schema.
V$ views queried expecting persistent history.
Forgetting the container in multitenant queries.
lessons.try_it: Find your session's current SQL in V$SESSION

lessons.title: Multitenant: CDBs and PDBs
concepts: Multitenant: one container database (CDB) hosts many pluggable databases (PDBs) — each PDB is a portable, isolated database sharing one instance's memory and processes. The 12c+ standard architecture.
CDB$ROOT holds Oracle metadata; PDB$SEED is the template; your data lives in PDBs. Connect to a PDB via its service name — the listener routes you to the right container.
Operations: CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE (from seed or clone), unplug/plug for moves and upgrades, relocate for near-zero-downtime migration. PDBs make fleet management sane.
Resource Manager plans cap PDB CPU/IO shares — noisy-neighbor control across tenants. Backup/recovery can target single PDBs — granularity the old architecture lacked.

example.walkthrough: v$pdbs lists every pluggable database and its state — the fleet overview.

pitfalls: Creating user data in CDB$ROOT.
Connecting to the CDB expecting PDB data.
Unplug/plug without checking compatibility.
lessons.try_it: List PDBs and their open modes

lessons.title: Security Architecture Primer
concepts: Users vs schemas: a user owns a schema; CREATE USER + GRANT CREATE SESSION is the minimum. Roles bundle privileges (CONNECT, RESOURCE are legacy — build least-privilege custom roles).
System privileges (CREATE TABLE) vs object privileges (SELECT ON hr.employees). Grant the minimum: WITH GRANT OPTION chains grants — audit who can re-grant.
Profiles enforce password policy (FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS, PASSWORD_LIFE_TIME); the DEFAULT profile is permissive — production needs a hardened profile.
Auditing: unified auditing tracks who did what (CREATE USER, ALTER TABLE, logons). Enable it before you need it — forensics after the fact is too late.

example.walkthrough: Least privilege in three lines: connect, then exactly one object privilege.

pitfalls: GRANT DBA 'to make it work'.
DEFAULT profile on production users.
WITH GRANT OPTION spreading silently.

lessons.title: Exam Format and Question Styles
concepts: The Oracle SQL exam tests recognition + application: stem describes a goal, options are code snippets or outcomes. Most questions are single-best-answer; a few are choose-two/three — read the stem's 'select' count first.

Question families map to domains: SELECT semantics (NULL, ROWNUM, GROUP BY), joins/subqueries, DDL constraints, single-row functions, and PL/SQL basics. Weight your study by family frequency, not by comfort.

Code-reading questions: trace execution order (FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY), not written order. Half the 'what does this return' questions die to execution-order mistakes.

Outcome questions ('which of these runs without error') reward error-code literacy: ORA-00979 (GROUP BY), ORA-00904 (bad identifier), ORA-01722 (bad number) — recognize the code, skip the re-derivation.

example.code:
-- stem: 'which returns the 3 highest salaries?'
-- A: WHERE ROWNUM<=3 ORDER BY sal DESC  -> wrong (rownum first)
-- B: subquery ORDER BY, outer ROWNUM filter -> right
-- C: ORDER BY sal FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY -> right
example.walkthrough: Two right answers exist in modern Oracle — the exam accepts both; know why A is the trap.

pitfalls: Answering before reading the 'select N' count.
Tracing code in written order.
Memorizing without understanding the trap pattern.
