lessons.title: High-Frequency Traps: NULL, ROWNUM, GROUP BY
concepts: NULL: any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN — = NULL never matches, NOT IN with a NULL returns nothing, COUNT(col) skips NULLs. One in five exam questions touches NULL semantics.
ROWNUM: assigned before ORDER BY — top-N needs the subquery wrap or FETCH FIRST. The exam's favorite wrong option is always the bare WHERE ROWNUM <= n ORDER BY.
GROUP BY: every non-aggregated SELECT item must be grouped (ORA-00979); WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups. 'Departments with >5 employees' = HAVING, never WHERE.
Aliases: usable in ORDER BY, invisible in WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING (they're computed in SELECT, which runs later). Referencing an alias early is a compile error.

example.walkthrough: The alias doesn't exist yet when WHERE runs — repeat the expression or restructure.

pitfalls: = NULL in a 'find the orphans' question.
ROWNUM-before-sort as the 'obvious' answer.
Alias referenced in WHERE or GROUP BY.
lessons.try_it: Write each trap correctly from memory

lessons.title: Joins and Subqueries Under Time Pressure
concepts: Join trigger phrases: 'including those with none' = LEFT JOIN; 'in A but not B' = MINUS or NOT EXISTS; 'for each X, its Y' = join or correlated subquery. Map the English to the construct in seconds.
EXISTS vs IN: EXISTS is NULL-safe and short-circuits — when the stem involves possible NULLs, EXISTS is the intended answer. NOT IN with NULLs is the trap.
Correlated vs non-correlated: 'per department' or 'for each employee' signals correlation or a GROUP BY. Scalar subqueries must return one row — 'more than one row' errors are the distractor.
Set operators: UNION dedups (costs a sort), UNION ALL doesn't; MINUS = 'but not'. Column counts must match — the exam slips in a mismatched branch as the wrong option.

example.walkthrough: NOT EXISTS (NULL-safe) and MINUS both express 'but not' — IN/NOT IN is the trap when NULLs lurk.

pitfalls: NOT IN over nullable columns.
UNION when the stem needs duplicates kept.
Correlated subquery where a join suffices.
lessons.try_it: Translate 10 English stems to constructs

lessons.title: DDL, Constraints, and Transactions
concepts: Constraint mapping: 'must reference an existing row' = FOREIGN KEY; 'unique values' = UNIQUE; 'limit the range' = CHECK; 'always filled' = NOT NULL; 'one identifier' = PRIMARY KEY. The stem's verb picks the constraint.
ON DELETE CASCADE vs default: default blocks parent deletion with children; CASCADE deletes them. The stem says which — 'blocked' vs 'also removed'.
Transaction questions: COMMIT makes permanent, ROLLBACK undoes to the last commit, SAVEPOINT enables partial rollback. DDL auto-commits — a CREATE TABLE mid-transaction commits your DML.
Views: simple views may be updatable; complex ones (joins, aggregates, DISTINCT) are read-only. 'Can you INSERT through this view?' hinges on complexity.

example.walkthrough: REFERENCES = existence guarantee; CHECK = domain list — the two most-tested constraints.

pitfalls: CHECK for cross-table existence.
Forgetting DDL's implicit commit.
INSERT through an aggregate view.
lessons.try_it: Design constraints for a 3-table schema

lessons.title: Functions and PL/SQL Quick Hits
concepts: Single-row function stems: 'first 3 characters' = SUBSTR, 'case-insensitive match' = UPPER both sides or function-based thinking, 'months between' = MONTHS_BETWEEN, 'replace missing with 0' = NVL/COALESCE.
Date formats: TO_DATE needs the exact format model; comparing DATE to string relies on NLS — the exam punishes implicit conversion assumptions.
PL/SQL quick hits: ELSIF (one word), SELECT ... INTO for single rows, %TYPE for anchoring, EXCEPTION blocks with WHEN OTHERS + RAISE, -20000..-20999 for RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR.
Cursor FOR loop = auto open/fetch/close; explicit cursors need all three steps. 'Which lines are missing' questions test the lifecycle.

example.walkthrough: %TYPE anchors the variable; INTO takes the single row; the handler covers the empty case.

pitfalls: ELSE IF instead of ELSIF.
SELECT without INTO in PL/SQL.
Custom error numbers outside -20000..-20999.
lessons.try_it: Drill 20 function-name flashcards

lessons.title: Full Mock Strategy and Review Loop
concepts: Mock protocol: strict timer, no notes, flag-and-return on time-sinks, educated guesses on all remaining (no penalty). Score by family to find the weakest domain, not just the total.
Review loop: for every miss, write the rule in one sentence ('ROWNUM assigns before ORDER BY') into a personal trap list. Re-mock until the trap list stops growing — that's mastery, not the score.
Second-pass technique: flagged questions get fresh eyes and remaining time; many 'hard' questions fall in 30 seconds on revisit. Never leave a flag unanswered.
Exam day: sleep beats cramming, arrive early, read each stem twice, watch for NOT/EXCEPT (negation flips the answer), and trust the trap list over gut feel.

example.code:
-- review log format
-- MISS: NOT IN returned nothing -> RULE: NOT IN + NULL = empty; use NOT EXISTS
-- MISS: picked ROWNUM-first -> RULE: sort first, limit second
example.walkthrough: The miss log converts errors into rules — each entry is a future point saved.

pitfalls: Re-taking mocks without reviewing misses.
Studying strengths instead of the weakest family.
Leaving flagged questions blank.

simulations.brief: A join between employees and orders returns far more rows than either table holds. The report is unusable and finance is waiting.
simulations.debrief: Row multiplication in a join means the join condition is wrong or missing — a cartesian product. The fix is always in the ON clause: match the foreign key to the primary key and re-check the grain.

evidence: SELECT e.name, o.product FROM employees e JOIN orders o ON e.dept = o.status
employees: 6 rows, orders: 6 rows, result: 14 rows

6 rows — one per order, with the right employee name

NULL handling: CASE (simple and searched forms) is ANSI, supports any condition (ranges, NULL checks, compound predicates), and nests cleanly.

Date arithmetic: for date math: ADD_MONTHS(date, n) handles month-end correctly (Jan 31 + 1 month = Feb 28/29). Explicit TO_DATE('2026-10-03','YYYY-MM-DD') or ANSI DATE '2026-10-03' literals are deterministic.
